papers.full_text: nature microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02489-y Comment Advancing equity through community-led, globally connected infectious disease research Pontiano Kaleebu, Aliya Naheed, Mahnaz Vahedi, Jackeline Alger, Lyda Osorio, Cristiani Vieira Machado, Francine Ntoumi, Mercedes Rumi, Mohammed AlKhaldi, Pacifique Ndishimye, Evelyn Gitau & Trudie Lang Platforms for community-led but globally connected knowledge and resource sharing can move us towards more equitable and more effective research and solutions for infectious diseases. The burden of infectious disease is vast and global, yet research capac- ity remains starkly unequal around the world. Most infectious disease research funding goes to high-income countries, where research agendas are set, studies led and benefits realized1. Meanwhile, major endemic diseases such as tuberculosis, malaria and cholera dispropor- tionately affect the poorest, least resourced communities, and newer or re-emerging threats such as Ebola, Zika and mpox occur in settings least equipped to respond. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored that research is the pathway out of a pandemic. This is just as true for tackling long-standing infec- tious diseases. An entire connected ecosystem encompassing different types of research is needed to make progress: basic and preclinical research to understand pathogens and host responses; observational studies to assess disease impact and guide public health strategies; infectious disease surveillance and modelling to monitor trends and inform responses; clinical trials to test safety and efficacy of vaccines, therapeutics or preventive public health measures; and social and behavioural research to understand community perceptions shap- ing health behaviours such as treatment-seeking and antibiotic use. When these clinical, social and laboratory sciences are possible in every setting, responses to infectious disease threats are fairer, faster and more effective. Knowledge exchange can help overcome persistent health research equity barriers Despite the clear need for connected and inclusive research glob- ally, multiple barriers prevent many of the places most affected by infectious diseases from being able to lead their own research. These include gaps in core research competencies, such as methods, data management, community engagement and communication, as well as ethics and integrity2. Moreover, fragmentation and short-term approaches are an issue for locally led research across disease areas and research modalities, highlighting a need for scientific skill devel- opment3. Capacity-strengthening efforts are often tied to individual research projects and limited-term funding. While these initiatives can build important skills, they may lack the continuity and adapt- ability needed to develop transferable competencies that support longer-term independent research4. Structural constraints, such as chronic under-resourcing of research systems, further impede the routine adoption of newer tools, including federated data analysis, novel trial designs and genomics-informed surveillance. Alongside the need to develop scientific skills and strengthen research systems, improved financing, infrastructure, workforce development, govern- ance and operational systems are needed to embed research into rou- tine healthcare delivery and enable local evidence generation with the potential to drive immediate improvements in local health outcomes. Giving health workers a mandate and strengthening local research systems can help address some parts of the cycle of dependency upon external parties. To respond to this issue and support locally led research in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), The Global Health Network (TGHN) was established in 2008. TGHN is a research practice-focused platform that was developed to aggregate, standard- ize and disseminate operational know-how across organizations, disci- plines, diseases and geographies, with the aim of helping individuals, groups and institutions move beyond dependency and one-off, focused projects into independent research. TGHN’s founding principle was to facilitate mobilization of research methods between researchers, and the platform is led through a franchise governance model with regional and country coordination. TGHN was first adopted in Africa, then rapidly developed into what is now a franchise community of more than 60 partners in more than 30 country centres across Latin America and the Caribbean, South and Southeast Asia and, more recently, the Middle East and North Africa. Each region locally coordinates its own agendas and priorities, and runs locally relevant in-person knowledge-sharing activities that provide ongoing mentoring and guidance, such as research clubs (regular peer-learning discussions), workshops (skills-based training) and topic-specific clinics (expert-led sessions on specific research chal- lenges). TGHN is accessed by more than 1.25 million researchers and health worker members globally. It works in partnership with global and regional initiatives, including the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), the European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership (EDCTP3) and the Science for Africa Foundation, among others, and is a World Health Organization (WHO) Collaborating Centre for knowledge mobilization and capacity strengthening. The vast, connected TGHN community offers practical, free materials and peer support that directly address the workforce, procedural and gov- ernance gaps left unresolved by short-term projects. Fundamentally, TGHN connects researchers and research organizations to ensure that a researcher in a LMIC has access to the same knowledge and opportuni- ties as peers in high-income countries. Upskilling the health research workforce To better enable research in communities and disease areas where evidence is lacking, TGHN addresses several of the barriers described above. These include gaps in core research competencies, fragmented Check for updates nature microbiology Comment capacity-strengthening efforts and limited local leadership in identify- ing and addressing research priorities. Franchise-style governance, as implemented by TGHN, enables regional hubs to lead activities, adapt materials to their own context and identify their priorities. Combined with access to shared tools, standard training curricula and centrally curated quality assurance guidance, this strengthens research competencies and gives local teams the mandate and confidence to develop context-appropriate protocols, lead continuing professional development and generate evidence that directly addresses their health needs. By expanding opportunities beyond high-income country research centres and senior clinicians, local custodians are better equipped to generate context-specific evidence, making the immediate implemen- tation of practice innovations more feasible. Embedded research for everyday diseases also enables teams to spot new threats. For example, during the mpox outbreak in the African Great Lakes region, TGHN members came together to report an unusual clinical presentation and transmission pattern for the disease, to connect researchers and funders, and to enable the deployment of international-standard pro- tocols. Skills training and cross-border sharing supported rapid, locally led evidence generation and raised awareness and understanding of what turned out to be a new strain5. Similarly, during the 2016 Zika outbreak in Latin America, local teams accessed multilingual training and community engagement frameworks. When mistrust and poor participant retention were jeopardizing pregnancy cohort studies, TGHN connected these teams directly with researchers in Malawi experienced in pregnancy research. The Malawi team shared their approaches of engaging community health workers, advisory groups and influential family members to build trust and community support. The Latin American teams adapted these approaches locally, overcom- ing mistrust and resolving the retention challenges, enabling the Zika studies to continue6. Genomics and data science have transformed research in wealthier nations; however, they remain underused in LMICs7,8. Enabling broader adoption of advanced technology and data science is also a key part of TGHN’s aim to overcome barriers to equitable research. Cutting-edge tools and methods need to be adapted to make them relevant, acces- sible and usable in LMICs. This involves not only transferring technol- ogy but also interpreting discoveries (such as new pathogen variants) within local epidemiological and social contexts to guide policy and practice. TGHN’s Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Knowledge Hub is one resource that exemplifies such an attempt. This free and open com- munity gives researchers, including those based in LMICs, a platform to connect with others gathering data to tackle AMR. High-quality resources and globally recommended protocols and methods, for example, from the WHO, are shared, enabling locally relevant data to inform local and global strategies. By June 2026, the AMR Knowl- edge Hub had 19,057 members who had downloaded more than 669 resources, and had run activities including symposia across Latin America, Africa and Asia during World AMR Awareness Week9. For example, the Accuracy and consequences of using trial-of-antibiotics for tuberculosis diagnosis (ACT TB) team in Malawi demonstrated through a randomized trial that routine broad-spectrum antibiotic use during tuberculosis investigation provided limited diagnostic benefit without improving clinical outcomes, supporting its discontinua- tion and improved antimicrobial stewardship. The team shared their protocols, standard operating procedures and regulatory and ethics materials through the Hub, enabling other research teams to directly reuse and adapt these approaches10. Enabling community involvement in setting pandemic and outbreak response research agendas During the COVID-19 pandemic, TGHN’s Knowledge Hub provided critical virtual support to LMIC researchers across seven thematic areas: intervention trials, diagnostics, disease characterization, social sciences, ethics and community engagement, vaccines and health systems. It offered curated free resources, articles, toolkits, funding guidance and e-learning. Specifically, more than 200,000 COVID-19 research resources were downloaded. A crowdsourcing initiative was also hosted to openly share study protocols, standard operating pro- cedures, consent forms and other tools adapted for immediate uptake and use across the globe. Partnerships with organizations such as CEPI, the Public Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Ethics Network (PHEPREN), the UK Public Health Rapid Support Team (UK-PHRST) and the COVID Neuro Network (Brain Infections Global) have enabled more than 65 multilingual webinars and workshops covering a broad range of COVID- 19 research topics, as these organizations knew they could engage with research teams in LMICs through our network. These were attended by more than 45,000 participants. CEPI also used TGHN as the access point for COVAX, the focal point for global vaccine access. Armed with access to this information and new connections, the Network’s partners and members ran studies to address new questions and used data tools they had not previously known existed. TGHN members are highly engaged, so this community also offers the opportunity to ask questions to better understand the perspectives and priorities of researchers and practitioners in LMICs. For exam- ple, in May 2020, a study was conducted to gauge the global research community’s agreement with the WHO COVID-19 research roadmap11. The research community’s priority questions differed from those in the WHO’s COVID Blueprint roadmap. TGHN brought these findings, together with perspectives from its ongoing working groups, into its advisory work with the UK Government during its G7 presidency, suc- cessfully using this evidence to argue for a focus on strengthening the wider research ecosystem rather than on trials and product develop- ment alone. This work led to World Health Assembly Resolution 75.8 on strengthening clinical trials, which reflected this broader focus12. This ‘crowdsourced’ approach is possible due to the size of the TGHN community, and provides a platform for the viewpoint of those from the regions and roles most affected but often not represented. Since this COVID-19 initiative, other organizations have also engaged the TGHN community to identify research priorities, while ensuring that the perspectives of researchers and health workers from underrepresented settings are included. For example, a recent global mixed-methods study gathered perspectives from 3,752 TGHN mem- bers to identify infectious diseases at risk of escalation and the factors driving these risks, providing evidence to inform the organization’s research priorities13. Working together for equitable research All researchers, regardless of location, should have the tools, guidance, support, networks and knowledge needed to conduct high-quality research. Many organizations, such as the WHO, the Special Pro- gramme for Research and training in Tropical Diseases (TDR), EDCTP3, CEPI, the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Well- come Trust and the Science for Africa Foundation, are also working to address these long-standing inequities, yet persistent barriers remain. Sustainable, flexible funding remains a critical need, par- ticularly for early-career researchers and for institutions without nature microbiology Comment long-standing donor ties. Structural inequities in authorship, lead- ership and research agenda-setting persist and must be dismantled. Weak infrastructure, the digital divide and limited access to scientific publishing continue to hold back progress, all well-documented and long-lamented disadvantages. By breaking down silos, upskilling the research workforce and linking marginalized communities to global resources, TGHN is actively working to address these barriers and create a fairer and more effective global health research ecosystem through the efforts of its global part- ners and members. Achieving this vision demands coordinated invest- ment across sectors: increased core funding for capacity-building in LMICs, partnerships that shift decision-making power, integration of research into health system planning, and stronger bridges between research, practice and policy. Sustaining and expanding these locally led, globally connected research communities can help ensure that the capacity to generate evidence exists where it is needed, enabling faster, more relevant and more equitable responses to current and future infectious disease threats. papers.title_original: Advancing equity through community-led, globally connected infectious disease research

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the global inequity in infectious disease research, particularly highlighting the disproportionate impact of diseases like mpox on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and the need for more equitable research practices.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a community-led, globally connected research platform called The Global Health Network (TGHN), which operates in multiple regions and countries, including Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, South and Southeast Asia, and the Middle East and North Africa. It focused on research teams in LMICs, particularly those working on mpox and other infectious diseases.
analysis.methods: The methods included establishing partnerships with global initiatives such as CEPI and PHEPREN, organizing multilingual webinars and workshops, and facilitating knowledge exchange to support local research capacity and independence.
analysis.main_results: The TGHN platform successfully enabled over 65 multilingual webinars and workshops on various infectious disease topics, including mpox, and connected research teams with expertise in specific areas like pregnancy cohort studies. It also supported a randomized trial demonstrating the limited diagnostic benefit of using broad-spectrum antibiotics for tuberculosis, which informed antimicrobial stewardship practices.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that collaborative, community-led research platforms can overcome systemic barriers and enable more effective, locally driven responses to infectious disease threats, including mpox. This approach is novel in its emphasis on embedding research into routine healthcare delivery and fostering local evidence generation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that strengthening local research systems and fostering partnerships can improve the detection and response to emerging infectious diseases like mpox, leading to more equitable and effective public health strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a single study and relies on reported outcomes from partnerships and webinars, which may lack direct, target-specific experimental data. However, the study provides a strong rationale for the importance of community-led research in addressing global health inequities.

analysis.summary_en: This study highlights the need for equitable and effective infectious disease research, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where diseases like mpox disproportionately affect communities. It describes the establishment of The Global Health Network (TGHN) as a community-led platform aimed at strengthening local research capacity and enabling independent, locally driven research. The methods involved partnerships with global initiatives, knowledge exchange, and capacity-building efforts. The main results include the successful organization of over 65 multilingual webinars and workshops, as well as a randomized trial showing limited diagnostic benefit of broad-spectrum antibiotics for tuberculosis. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that collaborative, community-led research can overcome systemic barriers and improve public health responses. The study suggests that such platforms can enhance the detection and management of infectious diseases like mpox, leading to more equitable health outcomes. However, the evidence is based on reported outcomes and partnerships, which may limit the strength of the findings.

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,加强本地研究体系并促进合作伙伴关系可以提高对像猴痘这样的新兴传染病的检测和应对能力,从而推动更加公平和有效的公共卫生策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 这些证据基于一项单一研究,并依赖于合作伙伴和网络研讨会报告的结果,这可能缺乏直接、针对性的实验数据。然而,该研究为社区主导研究在解决全球健康不平等问题中的重要性提供了有力的论据。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the global inequity in infectious disease research, particularly highlighting the disproportionate impact of diseases like mpox on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and the need for more equitable research practices.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study involved a community-led, globally connected research platform called The Global Health Network (TGHN), which operates in multiple regions and countries, including Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, South and Southeast Asia, and the Middle East and North Africa. It focused on research teams in LMICs, particularly those working on mpox and other infectious diseases.
analysis_en.methods: The methods included establishing partnerships with global initiatives such as CEPI and PHEPREN, organizing multilingual webinars and workshops, and facilitating knowledge exchange to support local research capacity and independence.
analysis_en.main_results: The TGHN platform successfully enabled over 65 multilingual webinars and workshops on various infectious disease topics, including mpox, and connected research teams with expertise in specific areas like pregnancy cohort studies. It also supported a randomized trial demonstrating the limited diagnostic benefit of using broad-spectrum antibiotics for tuberculosis, which informed antimicrobial stewardship practices.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that collaborative, community-led research platforms can overcome systemic barriers and enable more effective, locally driven responses to infectious disease threats, including mpox. This approach is novel in its emphasis on embedding research into routine healthcare delivery and fostering local evidence generation.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that strengthening local research systems and fostering partnerships can improve the detection and response to emerging infectious diseases like mpox, leading to more equitable and effective public health strategies.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a single study and relies on reported outcomes from partnerships and webinars, which may lack direct, target-specific experimental data. However, the study provides a strong rationale for the importance of community-led research in addressing global health inequities.

The burden of infectious disease is vast and global, yet research capac- ity remains starkly unequal around the world. Most infectious disease research funding goes to high-income countries, where research agendas are set, studies led and benefits realized1. Meanwhile, major endemic diseases such as tuberculosis, malaria and cholera dispropor- tionately affect the poorest, least resourced communities, and newer or re-emerging threats such as Ebola, Zika and mpox occur in settings least equipped to respond. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored that research is the pathway out of a pandemic. This is just as true for tackling long-standing infec- tious diseases. papers.title: SEIR+D epidemic modeling of infectious disease dynamics in Ebolowa, South Region, Republic of Cameroon
papers.abstract: Ebolowa, capital of Cameroon's South Region (≈ 92, 000 residents; referral hub for ≈ 180, 000), sits on the Cameroon–Gabon–Equatorial Guinea border and has recurrently faced cholera, malaria, Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), and mpox, yet its universal health coverage (UHC) service-coverage index is only 44/100 and physician density is under 2 per 10,000 population. We develop a generic, disease-agnostic SEIR+D framework rather than one fitted to a single pathogen: the baseline parameter set (R 0 = 3.00) represents a broadly plausible acute epidemic-prone infection, checked qualitatively—not calibrated—against 2021–2022 cholera surveillance data. Parameters are drawn from the World Health Organization (WHO) and national sources; R 0 is derived via the next-generation matrix method; and the resulting ODE system is solved via fourth-order Runge–Kutta integration over an 180-day horizon under three pre-specified intervention scenarios. At baseline, without intervention, infections peak at 14,226 persons (15.5% of the population) on day 119. The attack rate reaches 91.0% (≈ 83, 700 cases), 2,608 people die, and peak bed demand reaches 356% of the 200-bed capacity. A moderate non-pharmaceutical intervention (NPI, 40% transmission reduction from day 30) cuts the attack rate to 26.8% but still reaches 98% bed capacity. A strong NPI (70% reduction from day 20) cuts deaths by 99.8% (to ≈ 4) and holds bed utilization below 1%. The ten-day timing advantage over moderate NPI alone saves roughly 538 additional lives. These results indicate that only early, aggressive intervention is compatible with Ebolowa's health-system capacity, and that, given the city's four-decade epidemic history, funded, pre-positioned–rather than reactive mobilization after a signal emerges—is warranted for this cross-border population.

source_records.abstract: Ebolowa, capital of Cameroon's South Region (≈ 92, 000 residents; referral hub for ≈ 180, 000), sits on the Cameroon–Gabon–Equatorial Guinea border and has recurrently faced cholera, malaria, Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), and mpox, yet its universal health coverage (UHC) service-coverage index is only 44/100 and physician density is under 2 per 10,000 population. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估包括猴痘在内的传染病对埃博拉瓦市卫生系统的影响,并评估不同干预策略在减轻这些影响方面的有效性。该市有多种病原体反复暴发的历史,但其卫生系统容量仍然有限。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究采用SEIR+D流行病建模框架,模拟埃博拉瓦市的疾病动态,该市约有92,000居民,并作为约180,000人口的转诊中心。该模型通过2021–2022年的霍乱监测数据进行验证,代表了一种广泛可能的急性易爆发传染病。
elements_zh.methods: 模型参数来源于世界卫生组织和国家数据,R0通过下一代矩阵方法得出。采用四阶龙格-库塔积分法,在180天的时间范围内,模拟三种预设的干预情景,求解常微分方程(ODE)系统。
elements_zh.main_results: 在没有干预的情况下,模型预测感染人数将在第119天达到峰值,为14,226人(占人口的15.5%)。攻击率将达到91.0%(约83,700例病例),导致2,608人死亡,高峰期床位需求达到200床位容量的356%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,只有早期、强有力的干预措施才能与该市的卫生系统容量相匹配。他们强调,鉴于埃博拉瓦市有跨境暴发的历史,应优先考虑预先部署资源,而非在疫情信号出现后才采取的反应性措施。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,需要在埃博拉瓦市采取主动的公共卫生策略,特别是针对猴痘的暴发。它们强调了早期干预的重要性,以防止卫生系统超负荷运转。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究基于一个通用的SEIR+D模型,并通过霍乱数据进行校准,这可能无法完全代表猴痘的动态。证据强度中等,因为该模型并非专门针对猴痘,而是通过定性方式与相关数据进行验证。

papers.title: Educational Intervention Improves Antimicrobial Stewardship Knowledge but Reveals Persistent Barriers in Rural Hospitals
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Antimicrobial resistance threatens public health globally, and critical access hospitals (CAHs) serving rural communities face structural barriers to implementing antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs). This study evaluated whether a regional educational intervention could improve antimicrobial stewardship knowledge and implementation among rural healthcare professionals. Methods: A quantitative, quasi-experimental repeated cross-sectional evaluation was conducted following Antibiotic Stewardship conferences in 2023 and 2024. Participants from 38 rural and critical access hospitals completed pre-conference, post-conference, 6-month follow-up, and implementation surveys. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and unpaired chi-square tests, with Fisher’s exact test substituted where expected cell counts were below 5, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Seventy healthcare professionals participated across both years. Correct identification of the use of an antibiogram to guide empiric (rather than definitive) therapy improved from 27% pre-conference to 58% post-conference (p = 0.029). Confidence in antibiogram interpretation increased from 67% to 100% post-intervention (p = 0.004, Fisher’s exact) but declined to 50% (5 of 10) at 6-month follow-up. Knowledge of the minimum isolate threshold required to construct an antibiogram improved from 23% (7 of 30) pre-conference to 64% (7 of 11) at 6-month follow-up (p = 0.026, Fisher’s exact). Despite this, prescribing intent for conditions where antibiotics are typically unnecessary showed minimal improvement: recommendations for antibiotic use in middle ear infections decreased from 50% to 36.84%, and for mpox from 20% to 15.79%. All participants reported intent to modify clinical practice; however, time constraints, technology limitations, and lack of resources were consistently cited as primary barriers for implementation across both survey years. Conclusions: A regional educational intervention improved short-term antimicrobial stewardship knowledge and confidence among rural healthcare professionals, but knowledge retention declined over time and structural barriers persisted. Education alone is insufficient; sustained reinforcement and rural-adapted ASP models incorporating protected ASP time, decision-support tools and external partnerships are needed to translate knowledge gains into consistent stewardship practice.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the impact of a regional educational intervention on antimicrobial stewardship knowledge and practice among healthcare professionals in rural hospitals. The intervention improved knowledge and confidence in using antibiograms for empiric therapy and understanding isolate thresholds, but these gains were not sustained at 6-month follow-up. Prescribing intent for unnecessary antibiotic use showed minimal improvement. Despite the educational efforts, structural barriers such as time constraints, technology limitations, and lack of resources remained significant. The study highlights the need for sustained reinforcement and tailored stewardship models to translate knowledge into consistent practice. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the absence of long-term follow-up data and limited information on generalizability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 抗菌药物耐药性威胁全球公共卫生,而为农村社区提供服务的临界接入医院(CAHs)在实施抗菌药物管理计划(ASPs)方面面临结构性障碍。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究评估了区域性教育干预是否能改善农村医疗专业人员的抗菌药物合理使用知识和实施情况。来自38家农村和临界接入医院的参与者完成了会前、会后、6个月随访和实施调查。
elements_zh.methods: 在2023年和2024年的抗菌药物管理会议后,进行了一项定量、准实验的重复横断面评估。定量数据使用描述性统计和非配对卡方检验进行分析,当预期单元格计数低于5时,使用Fisher精确检验,显著性水平设为p < 0.05。
elements_zh.main_results: 两年间共有70名医疗专业人员参与。正确识别抗菌图谱用于指导经验性(而非确定性)治疗的比例从会前的27%提高到会后的58%(p = 0.029)。抗菌图谱解读的信心从会前的67%提升到会后的100%(p = 0.004,Fisher精确检验),但在6个月随访时下降至50%(10人中有5人)。关于构建抗菌图谱所需的最低分离株阈值的知识,从会前的23%(30人中有7人)提高到6个月随访时的64%(11人中有7人)(p = 0.026,Fisher精确检验)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 区域性教育干预改善了农村医疗专业人员在短期内的抗菌药物合理使用知识和信心,但知识保持随时间下降,结构性障碍依然存在。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,尽管教育可以增强知识,但需要持续强化以及针对农村环境的抗菌药物管理模型,以应对持续存在的障碍并改善一致的抗菌药物管理实践。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 所提供的证据未报告干预在6个月随访期之后的长期效果,也未提供结果在其他医疗环境中的可推广性信息。

papers.title_zh: 教育干预改善抗菌药物合理使用知识但揭示农村医院中持续存在的障碍
papers.source_body_en: Background/Objectives: Antimicrobial resistance threatens public health globally, and critical access hospitals (CAHs) serving rural communities face structural barriers to implementing antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs). This study evaluated whether a regional educational intervention could improve antimicrobial stewardship knowledge and implementation among rural healthcare professionals. Methods: A quantitative, quasi-experimental repeated cross-sectional evaluation was conducted following Antibiotic Stewardship conferences in 2023 and 2024. Participants from 38 rural and critical access hospitals completed pre-conference, post-conference, 6-month follow-up, and implementation surveys. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and unpaired chi-square tests, with Fisher’s exact test substituted where expected cell counts were below 5, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Seventy healthcare professionals participated across both years. Correct identification of the use of an antibiogram to guide empiric (rather than definitive) therapy improved from 27% pre-conference to 58% post-conference (p = 0.029). Confidence in antibiogram interpretation increased from 67% to 100% post-intervention (p = 0.004, Fisher’s exact) but declined to 50% (5 of 10) at 6-month follow-up. Knowledge of the minimum isolate threshold required to construct an antibiogram improved from 23% (7 of 30) pre-conference to 64% (7 of 11) at 6-month follow-up (p = 0.026, Fisher’s exact). Despite this, prescribing intent for conditions where antibiotics are typically unnecessary showed minimal improvement: recommendations for antibiotic use in middle ear infections decreased from 50% to 36.84%, and for mpox from 20% to 15.79%. All participants reported intent to modify clinical practice; however, time constraints, technology limitations, and lack of resources were consistently cited as primary barriers for implementation across both survey years. Conclusions: A regional educational intervention improved short-term antimicrobial stewardship knowledge and confidence among rural healthcare professionals, but knowledge retention declined over time and structural barriers persisted. Education alone is insufficient; sustained reinforcement and rural-adapted ASP models incorporating protected ASP time, decision-support tools and external partnerships are needed to translate knowledge gains into consistent stewardship practice.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景/目标:抗菌药物耐药性威胁全球公共卫生,而为农村社区提供服务的临界接入医院(CAHs)在实施抗菌药物管理计划(ASPs)方面面临结构性障碍。本研究评估了区域性教育干预是否能改善农村医疗专业人员的抗菌药物合理使用知识和实施情况。方法:在2023年和2024年的抗菌药物管理会议后,进行了一项定量、准实验的重复横断面评估。来自38家农村和临界接入医院的参与者完成了会前、会后、6个月随访和实施调查。定量数据使用描述性统计和非配对卡方检验进行分析,当预期单元格计数低于5时,使用Fisher精确检验,显著性水平设为p < 0.05。结果:两年间共有70名医疗专业人员参与。正确识别抗菌图谱用于指导经验性(而非确定性)治疗的比例从会前的27%提高到会后的58%(p = 0.029)。抗菌图谱解读的信心从会前的67%提升到会后的100%(p = 0.004,Fisher精确检验),但在6个月随访时下降至50%(10人中有5人)。关于构建抗菌图谱所需的最低分离株阈值的知识,从会前的23%(30人中有7人)提高到6个月随访时的64%(11人中有7人)(p = 0.026,Fisher精确检验)。尽管如此,对于通常不需要抗生素的疾病,处方意图的改善非常有限:中耳感染中抗生素使用的推荐比例从50%下降至36.84%,对于猴痘的推荐比例从20%下降至15.79%。所有参与者都表示有意修改临床实践;然而,时间限制、技术限制和资源不足被一致认为是实施过程中持续存在的主要障碍。结论:区域性教育干预改善了农村医疗专业人员在短期内的抗菌药物合理使用知识和信心,但知识保持随时间下降,结构性障碍依然存在。仅靠教育是不够的;需要持续强化以及结合受保护的ASPs时间、决策支持工具和外部合作的农村适应型ASPs模型,才能将知识提升转化为一致的抗菌药物管理实践。

papers.full_text: Dear Editor, Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) is coming of age and is poised to develop into a serious candidate for Point‐of‐care diagnostics. RPA has been around for almost 20 years. Originally developed by academics Nial Armes and Olaf Piepenburg, it was first published in 2006, and a first patent was issued in 2007. In the first decade of the 2000s, several isothermal molecular amplification methods emerged [1] but real‐time RPA stood out at the time as its design format was reminiscent of real‐time PCR (two primers and a probe). The probe used to confirm specific amplification was intuitively easier to accept than the backfolding FIP/BIB primers of Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP), which in essence do the same. To this day, this misunderstanding of the LAMP mechanism still leads to the development of additional real‐time probe system for LAMP in order to add a confirmatory probe [2, 3, 4, 5]. This may, however, also be the case because of the well‐documented unspecific amplification issues of LAMP [6]. In terms of sensitivity, both LAMP and RPA have been shown to be as sensitive as real‐time PCR in numerous studies; RT‐RPA, however, sometimes struggles in the last decade of sensitivity. An intriguing recent analysis speculates that, in contrast to fully biphasic UvsX‐GP32 droplets formed in the RPA reaction, the addition of RT leads to fully miscible droplets including BsuI, which inhibits UvsX and thus may cause the loss of sensitivity in RT‐RPA [7]. Both LAMP and RPA struggle with one tube multiplexing but the introduction of cascade amplification using CRISPR/Cas12 and 13 systems which digest ssDNA or ssRNA reports offers solutions but the most promising appear to be spatial multiplexing concepts on surfaces or digital droplets. From the onset RPA was available in lyophilised pellets for DNA and RNA targets which made it a popular choice for research into cold chain independent point of care diagnostics [8]. Other features included the speed of amplification to the analytical limit of detection from 5 to 20 min at very low temperatures. The low reaction temperature generically implies a reduced engineering effort and associated costs for a POCT device and even inspired some assay developments with body heat driven RPA [9]. Over the years RPA was implemented in a plethora of microfluidic devices [10]. During the Covid pandemic, widespread testing outside of centralised laboratories provided advantages for general epidemic control and contact tracing in particular and has changed attitudes towards POCT [11]. Subsequently, the FDA invited the diagnostic industry to submit tests for home testing and most recently approved a PCR home test by US Company Visby Medical Inc. for sexually transmitted diseases. It uses a disposable heavily engineered “device‐cartridge” with embedded electronics to steer a continuous flow heated serpentine PCR channel which seems a waste to dispose of after one test (patent US20250128262A1). Another disposable electronics concept was the much simpler LUCIRA device for a SARS‐CoV‐2 LAMP assay [12]. Marketed as device‐free disposable tests, both POCTs in truth generate electronic waste and do not meet the last E in the RERASSURED criteria which stands for “Equipment free or simple environmentally friendly” [13]. Only recently cost efficient and scalable simple multi use POCT devices have emerged such as the CPod (CRISPR assay [14]), minoo (RPA assay [15]), and Pebble device (LAMP assay [16]). CPod and minoo use a Light Emitting Diode (LED) and the onboard multi‐spectral digital sensor AS7341, for fluorescence detection while the Pebble uses a mini digital camera to detect a colorimetric reaction. The minoo device received CE‐IVD legacy certification in May 2022 for a SARS‐CoV‐2 RT‐RPA assay using a simple extraction procedure for throat swabs. While many others have created similar direct extraction concepts e.g., using TCEP buffer for SHERLOCK and LAMP assays [17, 18, 19], the bottleneck extraction for more complicated sample types is still not solved. In terms of multiplexing, the Biofire FilmArray system for multiplex PCR [20] has already demonstrated that spatial multiplexing is preferential to one‐pot multiplexing, which is true for the workload needed to balance one‐pot reactions and for the verification and validation effort for one‐pot reactions versus spatially separated individual reactions. It is therefore to be expected that the simple multi use POCT devices will also move in this direction. Only a few device publications have listed cost of goods (CoGS) for isothermal and portable PCR devices (range 50–193$ per device [21, 22]), therefore, with a margin added it is safe to estimate the CoGs within 250€ for the above devices. They can be categorized as environmentally friendly as at least the minoo device was verified to be functional for at least 1000 runs [15]. If they solve the extraction issue, these simple readers could help to provide molecular diagnostics for infectious agents to the 47% of the global population that has little to no access to diagnostics at all, thus solving the last mile problem in providing access to diagnostics close to the patient [23]. In principle, these test platforms would be deliverable to users at reduced sales prices if upscaled production was outsourced to international electronics/mobile phone manufacturers. Local biochemistry production would allow dissemination of affordable respective assays close to the WHO requirement of 1$/test [13]. In comparison, current microfluidic and microsystem POCT systems in general fail to consider the economy of scale for mass production and market [24]. RPA has been rated as the most promising isothermal molecular amplification technique since it utilizes unmodified oligonucleotides, rapidly amplifies targets at only slightly elevated temperature without compromising the stringency of amplification, and uses probe‐based target verification in its real time format [1]. A meta‐analysis of molecular POC assays for SARS‐CoV‐2 concluded that seven RT‐RPA/RAA assays achieved detection sensitivity level similar to diagnosis on purified RNA samples by PCR from crude patient samples [25]. RPA was used in multiple field studies in mobile laboratories and produced sufficient evidence demonstrating that the performance of RPA is suitable for point of care use. In view of original RPA patents running out in 2026 the first open‐source protocols for RPA mix production have been published [26, 27]. Apart from the original Twist DX kit which currently is not available for RNA detection, three RPA copy chemistries are available in China: Recombinase Aided Amplification (RAA [28], Qitian, https://en.qt‐bio.com/Pro/12.html), Enzymatic Recombinase Amplification (ERA [29], GenDX, https://www.igeneye.com/), and Multienzyme Isothermal Rapid Amplification (MIRA [30], Amp‐Future Biotech Co. Ltd. https://www.amp‐futurebio.com/products). The impetus to copy the successful RPA concept goes even as far as claiming to have invented a probe system which is identical to the one originally published in 2006 [31]. In the area of lateral flow detection RPA is beginning to overtake LAMP with 490 publications versus 412 recorded on PubMed. Taken together RPA is catching up on LAMP (Figure 1) and has the potential to develop into a serious candidate for POCT implementation which is certainly the view in Asia as 61% of RPA publications originate from China alone. papers.title_original: Point of Care Testing and Recombinase Polymerase Amplification

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the potential of Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) as a point-of-care (POCT) diagnostic tool, particularly in comparison to other isothermal amplification methods like LAMP, and to address the challenges in achieving sensitive and scalable POCT solutions for infectious diseases.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study reviewed existing literature and analyzed the design, performance, and application of RPA and related isothermal amplification methods in the context of POCT, focusing on their sensitivity, multiplexing capabilities, and environmental impact. It also examined the development of POCT devices for various pathogens, including SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.methods: The study evaluated the methods used in RPA and LAMP assays, including their sensitivity, multiplexing strategies, and the use of electronic components in POCT devices. It also considered the cost of goods for these devices and their environmental impact based on available literature.

papers.title_zh: 床边检测与重组酶聚合酶扩增
papers.source_body_en: In the first decade of the 2000s, several isothermal molecular amplification methods emerged [1] but real‐time RPA stood out at the time as its design format was reminiscent of real‐time PCR (two primers and a probe). Dear Editor, Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) is coming of age and is poised to develop into a serious candidate for Point‐of‐care diagnostics. RPA has been around for almost 20 years. Originally developed by academics Nial Armes and Olaf Piepenburg, it was first published in 2006, and a first patent was issued in 2007. The probe used to confirm specific amplification was intuitively easier to accept than the backfolding FIP/BIB primers of Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP), which in essence do the same. To this day, this misunderstanding of the LAMP mechanism still leads to the development of additional real‐time probe system for LAMP in order to add a confirmatory probe [2, 3, 4, 5]. This may, however, also be the case because of the well‐documented unspecific amplification issues of LAMP [6]. In terms of sensitivity, both LAMP and RPA have been shown to be as sensitive as real‐time PCR in numerous studies; RT‐RPA, however, sometimes struggles in the last decade of sensitivity. An intriguing recent analysis speculates that, in contrast to fully biphasic UvsX‐GP32 droplets formed in the RPA reaction, the addition of RT leads to fully miscible droplets including BsuI, which inhibits UvsX and thus may cause the loss of sensitivity in RT‐RPA [7]. Both LAMP and RPA struggle with one tube multiplexing but the introduction of cascade amplification using CRISPR/Cas12 and 13 systems which digest ssDNA or ssRNA reports offers solutions but the most promising appear to be spatial multiplexing concepts on surfaces or digital droplets. This initiative is part of broader efforts to combat mpox disease, which is caused by the monkeypox virus (Orthopoxvirus monkeypox). The evidence highlights the WHO's commitment to ensuring equitable vaccine distribution, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported. The initiative is confirmed as an official public health action, with no further details on testing, containment, or risk assessment provided. The event is described as a global effort, targeting populations affected by mpox across multiple countries.

What Older Adults Need to Know Physical Health Sep 02, 2026 11 min read Print Page Share Related Topics Prevention Physical Health Monkeypox, now officially called mpox, is a viral disease caused by the monkeypox virus. It can spread from person to person and typically causes a rash and other flu-like symptoms. Mpox is sometimes confused with shingles because both illnesses cause painful skin bumps and fluid-filled blisters. While the risk of mpox to the general public remains low, recent cases have been linked with travel to regions where outbreaks are occurring or close contact with someone who has mpox. Here’s what you need to know about the mpox virus, symptoms of mpox illness, how it spreads, and who is most at risk. Mpox Quick Facts What is mpox? A contagious illness caused by the monkeypox virus How does it spread? Mainly through close contact with someone who has mpox Common symptoms Rash, fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, and body aches How long does it last? Most people recover within 2–4 weeks Who is at higher risk? People with certain immune conditions and other risk factors Is it serious? Most cases are mild, but serious illness can occur Is there a vaccine? Yes, vaccination is recommended for certain people at higher risk What if I'm exposed? Contact a health care provider promptly for guidance What is the history of mpox (monkeypox)? The mpox virus was discovered in a Denmark laboratory in 1958 when several laboratory monkeys developed a pox-like rash. The first report of a human contracting mpox was in 1970, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Public health officials say the disease is endemic in some central and west African countries, and prior to the 2022 outbreak, mpox cases in the United States were “linked to international travel to countries where the disease commonly occurs or through imported animals.” What's the difference between clade I and clade II mpox? There are two main types of the monkeypox virus, known as clade I and clade II. A clade refers to a group of closely related viruses. Clade I has historically circulated in Central Africa and is generally associated with more severe illness and a higher risk of death. It may also spread more easily. Clade II has historically circulated in West Africa and generally causes less severe illness and fewer deaths than clade I. A subtype of clade II caused the global mpox outbreak that began in 2022. Is there an mpox outbreak in the U.S.? Not currently. But there was a rare mpox outbreak back in 2022. On May 18, 2022, the United States recorded the year’s first case of mpox. By late September, while older adults were rolling up their sleeves for an updated COVID-19 vaccine, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) had tallied 24,572 confirmed mpox cases. Since the peak of the mpox outbreak in 2022, the highest monthly case counts occurred in the fall of 2025. Today, clade II mpox is still circulating at low levels nationally, and cases of clade I are rising as of July 2026 according to CDC. How does mpox spread? Mpox is transmitted through “close, personal, often skin-to-skin contact,” CDC says. This includes direct contact with mpox rash, scabs, or body fluids from a person with mpox; touching objects, fabrics (clothing, bedding, or towels), and surfaces that have been used by someone with mpox; and contact with respiratory secretions. Mpox is zoonotic, which means animals can transmit it to people, but “monkeys are not a main source of transmission,” Yale University epidemiologist Saad Omer said in an interview with the Yale School of Medicine. “... it’s the rodents that we need to worry about in terms of actual transmission.” In the U.S. in 2003, there were 47 “confirmed and probable” mpox cases linked to contact with pet prairie dogs, who arrived in a shipment of mammals that included several types of rodents. What caused the 2022 mpox outbreak? Researchers discovered that during the 2022-2023 mpox outbreak, the Clade IIb genetic sub-lineage of the virus adapted to efficiently spread primarily through close, intimate physical contact, mainly within interconnected sexual networks. As of June 12, 2024, more than 97,000 confirmed mpox cases had been reported across 118 countries as part of the global outbreak that began in 2022.1 Is mpox life-threatening? Mpox is rarely fatal, and more than 99% of people who get it survive. But the risk of serious illness may be higher for people with weakened immune systems, young children, people with a history of eczema, and those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. When the Los Angeles, California, Department of Health reported the country’s first death to mpox in mid-September 2022, officials said the person who succumbed to the virus was “severely immunocompromised.” Is mpox dangerous for oldera dults? Through Sept. 22, 2022, demographic data show that confirmed mpox cases for adults ages 61 and older were among the lowest recorded. CDC reported 277 cases in that age group. CDC does not cite older age in itself as a risk factor for older adults, but public health officials stressed that anyone who’s had close, personal contact with someone who has mpox is at risk. Who is at highest risk for mpox? Following the 2022-2023 mpox outbreak, a review of 31 studies found that the risk of getting mpox was higher among people who had close contact with an infected person or animal, had multiple sexual partners or unprotected sex, or had HIV or another sexually transmitted infection. Men who have sex with men also had a higher risk of infection in the populations studied.2 What are the symptoms of mpox? A rash, sometimes painful, is the most common symptom of the mpox virus. It can appear and spread on or near the genitals or anus, or on other areas of the body like the hands, feet, chest, face, or mouth. The mpox rash goes through several stages, including scabs, before healing. Flu-like symptoms are other signs of infection. These can include: Fever Chills Swollen lymph nodes Exhaustion Muscle aches and backache Headache Respiratory symptoms. If you think you have symptoms or have been in close contact with someone who has the virus, talk to your doctor about whether you should be tested. If you have been exposed, watch for mpox symptoms for 21 days from the date of exposure. How do you prevent mpox? You can help protect yourself and others by following these CDC-provided guidelines: Avoid close, skin-to-skin contact with people who have a rash that looks like mpox. Do not touch the rash or scabs of a person with mpox. Do not kiss, hug, cuddle, or have sex with someone with mpox. Avoid contact with objects and materials that a person with mpox has used. Don’t share eating utensils or cups with a person with mpox. Don’t handle or touch the bedding, towels, or clothing of a person with mpox. Wash your hands often with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer, especially before eating or touching your face and after you use the bathroom. What if I get mpox? “Currently there is no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved treatment specifically for monkeypox,” CDC says. “For most patients with monkeypox who don't have severe disease or risk factors for severe disease (e.g., severe immunocompromise), supportive care and pain control will help them recover.” Even without a specific mpox treatment, there are a number of ways to manage your symptoms, including getting plenty of rest. Most people recover within 2-4 weeks. Should I get an mpox vaccine? CDC says, “If you have certain risk factors that make you eligible, you can help protect yourself from monkeypox by getting the 2-dose monkeypox vaccine.” Talk to your health care professional or local health department to learn more about JYNNEOS, the two-dose vaccine developed to protect against smallpox and mpox. How to stay informed about mpox You can keep up with mpox developments and guidance on the CDC website, a trusted source for information on topics ranging from mpox prevention to mpox treatment. Data is updated frequently. WHO offers a comprehensive FAQ and a global perspective. And as always, if you have any health concerns, talk to your doctor. You can also take steps to protect your overall health by staying up to date on your flu, COVID, and RSV vaccines. Learn more about the vaccines recommended for older adults. Sources 1. Rajesh Yadav, et. al., Mpox 2022 to 2025 Update: A Comprehensive Review on Its Complications, Transmission, Diagnosis, and Treatment. Viruses. May 25, 2025. Found on the internet at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12197743/ 2. Chigozie Louisa Jane Ugwu, et. al., Risk factors associated with human Mpox infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Global Health. February 3, 2025. Found on the internet at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11795413/ Share Related Topics Prevention Physical Health Is It Flu or COVID? While flu and COVID-19 share many similarities, they are distinct illnesses with different causes, complications, and treatments. Today, clade II mpox is still circulating at low levels nationally, and cases of clade I are rising as of July 2026 according to CDC. How does mpox spread? Mpox is transmitted through “close, personal, often skin-to-skin contact,” CDC says. This includes direct contact with mpox rash, scabs, or body fluids from a person with mpox; touching objects, fabrics (clothing, bedding, or towels), and surfaces that have been used by someone with mpox; and contact with respiratory secretions. Mpox is zoonotic, which means animals can transmit it to people, but “monkeys are not a main source of transmission,” Yale University epidemiologist Saad Omer said in an interview with the Yale School of Medicine. “... it’s the rodents that we need to worry about in terms of actual transmission.” In the U.S. in 2003, there were 47 “confirmed and probable” mpox cases linked to contact with pet prairie dogs, who arrived in a shipment of mammals that included several types of rodents. What caused the 2022 mpox outbreak? Researchers discovered that during the 2022-2023 mpox outbreak, the Clade IIb genetic sub-lineage of the virus adapted to efficiently spread primarily through close, intimate physical contact, mainly within interconnected sexual networks. As of June 12, 2024, more than 97,000 confirmed mpox cases had been reported across 118 countries as part of the global outbreak that began in 2022.1 Is mpox life-threatening? Mpox is rarely fatal, and more than 99% of people who get it survive. But the risk of serious illness may be higher for people with weakened immune systems, young children, people with a history of eczema, and those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. When the Los Angeles, California, Department of Health reported the country’s first death to mpox in mid-September 2022, officials said the person who succumbed to the virus was “severely immunocompromised.” Is mpox dangerous for oldera dults? Through Sept. 22, 2022, demographic data show that confirmed mpox cases for adults ages 61 and older were among the lowest recorded. CDC reported 277 cases in that age group. CDC does not cite older age in itself as a risk factor for older adults, but public health officials stressed that anyone who’s had close, personal contact with someone who has mpox is at risk. Who is at highest risk for mpox? Following the 2022-2023 mpox outbreak, a review of 31 studies found that the risk of getting mpox was higher among people who had close contact with an infected person or animal, had multiple sexual partners or unprotected sex, or had HIV or another sexually transmitted infection. Men who have sex with men also had a higher risk of infection in the populations studied.2 What are the symptoms of mpox? A rash, sometimes painful, is the most common symptom of the mpox virus. It can appear and spread on or near the genitals or anus, or on other areas of the body like the hands, feet, chest, face, or mouth. The mpox rash goes through several stages, including scabs, before healing. Flu-like symptoms are other signs of infection. These can include: Fever Chills Swollen lymph nodes Exhaustion Muscle aches and backache Headache Respiratory symptoms. If you think you have symptoms or have been in close contact with someone who has the virus, talk to your doctor about whether you should be tested. If you have been exposed, watch for mpox symptoms for 21 days from the date of exposure. How do you prevent mpox? You can help protect yourself and others by following these CDC-provided guidelines: Avoid close, skin-to-skin contact with people who have a rash that looks like mpox. Do not touch the rash or scabs of a person with mpox. Do not kiss, hug, cuddle, or have sex with someone with mpox. Avoid contact with objects and materials that a person with mpox has used. Don’t share eating utensils or cups with a person with mpox. Don’t handle or touch the bedding, towels, or clothing of a person with mpox. Wash your hands often with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer, especially before eating or touching your face and after you use the bathroom. What if I get mpox? “Currently there is no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved treatment specifically for monkeypox,” CDC says. “For most patients with monkeypox who don't have severe disease or risk factors for severe disease (e.g., severe immunocompromise), supportive care and pain control will help them recover.” Even without a specific mpox treatment, there are a number of ways to manage your symptoms, including getting plenty of rest. Most people recover within 2-4 weeks. Should I get an mpox vaccine? CDC says, “If you have certain risk factors that make you eligible, you can help protect yourself from monkeypox by getting the 2-dose monkeypox vaccine.” Talk to your health care professional or local health department to learn more about JYNNEOS, the two-dose vaccine developed to protect against smallpox and mpox. How to stay informed about mpox You can keep up with mpox developments and guidance on the CDC website, a trusted source for information on topics ranging from mpox prevention to mpox treatment. Data is updated frequently. WHO offers a comprehensive FAQ and a global perspective. And as always, if you have any health concerns, talk to your doctor. You can also take steps to protect your overall health by staying up to date on your flu, COVID, and RSV vaccines. Learn more about the vaccines recommended for older adults. Sources 1. The text explains that mpox is a viral disease caused by the monkeypox virus, which can spread through close contact with an infected person or animal. Common symptoms include a rash, fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, and body aches, with most people recovering within 2–4 weeks. The article notes that while the risk to the general public remains low, recent cases have been linked to travel to regions with outbreaks or close contact with infected individuals. The article emphasizes that people with certain immune conditions or risk factors, such as multiple sexual partners or HIV, are at higher risk. It recommends vaccination for high-risk individuals and advises seeking medical guidance if exposed. The text does not provide specific details on current investigation status or containment measures.

news.title_zh: 猴痘(猴痘):症状、传播方式及预防措施——全国老年事务委员会(NCOA)
news.source_body_en: The article from The National Council on Aging (NCOA) published on September 2, 2026, provides general information about mpox (monkeypox), including its symptoms, transmission, prevention, and risk factors for older adults. It is a guidance article, not an outbreak report. The text explains that mpox is a viral disease caused by the monkeypox virus, which can spread through close contact with an infected person or animal. Common symptoms include a rash, fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, and body aches, with most people recovering within 2–4 weeks. The article notes that while the risk to the general public remains low, recent cases have been linked to travel to regions with outbreaks or close contact with infected individuals. It also highlights that clade I is associated with more severe illness and higher mortality, while clade II generally causes less severe symptoms. As of June 12, 2024, over 97,000 confirmed mpox cases were reported globally. The article emphasizes that people with certain immune conditions or risk factors, such as multiple sexual partners or HIV, are at higher risk. It recommends vaccination for high-risk individuals and advises seeking medical guidance if exposed. The text does not provide specific details on current investigation status or containment measures.
news.content_zh: 全国老年事务委员会(NCOA)于2026年9月2日发布的一篇文章提供了关于猴痘(猴痘)的一般信息,包括其症状、传播、预防措施以及老年人的风险因素。这是一篇指导性文章,而非暴发报告。文章指出,猴痘是一种由猴痘病毒引起的病毒性疾病,可通过与感染者或动物的密切接触传播。常见症状包括皮疹、发热、寒战、淋巴结肿大、头痛和身体疼痛,大多数患者在2–4周内康复。文章提到,尽管对一般公众的风险仍然较低,但近期病例与前往暴发地区或与感染者密切接触有关。它还强调,I型毒株与更严重的疾病和更高的死亡率相关,而II型毒株通常引起较轻的症状。截至2024年6月12日,全球已报告超过97,000例确认的猴痘病例。文章指出,某些免疫状况或风险因素较高的人群,如有多名性伴侣或HIV感染者,感染风险更高。它建议高风险人群进行疫苗接种,并建议在暴露后及时寻求医疗指导。文章未提供当前调查状态或防控措施的具体细节。

analysis.location_and_population: The UK, Canada, Uganda, and India are mentioned as locations affected by mpox. The mpox clade Ib variant is spreading globally, with specific mention of Africa and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The affected population includes travellers, healthcare facilities, and the general public.
analysis.event: Canada confirmed its first case of mpox clade I virus in a traveller from Africa. The WHO and Africa CDC launched a 'Joint Continental Response Plan' to address the mpox outbreak.

Mpox vaccination campaigns have started in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with the first batch of 1 lakh doses arriving.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Authorities are monitoring the spread of the new mpox variant in the UK. The WHO and Africa CDC have launched a 'Joint Continental Response Plan' for mpox response efforts. Mpox vaccination campaigns have begun in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The Indian government has issued guidelines to curb the spread of mpox in the country.

analysis.brief_en: The news report highlights the global spread of the mpox virus, particularly the clade Ib variant, which has caused 17 deaths in Africa and 164 infections in Uganda. The UK confirmed a new mpox variant in a traveller from Asia, while Canada reported its first case of mpox clade I virus in a traveller returning from Africa. The WHO and Africa CDC have launched a 'Joint Continental Response Plan' to address the outbreak, starting in September 2024 and ending in February 2025. In response, the Indian government issued detailed guidelines for all states and Union Territories to prevent further spread. Mpox vaccination campaigns have begun in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with the first batch of 1 lakh doses arriving. The report also discusses the potential for mpox to cause a pandemic, similar to the previous COVID-19 outbreak, and the implementation of pandemic-like restrictions in airports and hospitals. These measures aim to control the spread and manage the health risks associated with the mpox virus.

Breadcrumb Home What UNICEF Does Children's Health Mpox https://www.unicefusa.org/what-unicef-does/childrens-health/mpox A new variant of mpox, or monkeypox, is killing children in Africa. What causes this disease, and who is at risk? The answers to these and other frequently asked questions. Updated Sept. 2, 2026 What is mpox? Mpox, also known as monkeypox, is an infectious disease caused by an orthopoxvirus. It can spread from animals to people and from person to person. Cases of mpox are most often found in areas with tropical rainforests, home to squirrels, monkeys and other small mammals that are susceptible. The virus was discovered in 1958 in Denmark in monkeys kept for research. The first reported human case of mpox was in 1970, in a 9-month-old boy in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. There are two genetic clades of the virus, clade I and clade II. Clade I mpox tends to cause a higher number of severe infections and have a higher mortality rate than clade II mpox. Most deaths occur in children. Related: Children account for half of suspected mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau How prevalent is mpox? Mpox remains a significant and ongoing global health burden. From Jan. 1, 2022 through July 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190,683 confirmed cases of mpox and 529 deaths. Roughly two-thirds of reported cases were in Africa. In 2022, there was a global outbreak of clade II mpox, which led to more than 95,000 cases across 115 non-endemic countries. The 2024 outbreak was a clade I outbreak. An upsurge of mpox cases in the DRC that year was driven by outbreaks associated with two variants of clade I, clade Ia and clade Ib. What are the symptoms of mpox? Mpox causes symptoms that are similar to smallpox, though less severe. Symptoms include skin rash, fever, sore throat, headache, body aches, back pain, low energy and swollen lymph nodes. Some people who contract mpox get very sick. Most people fully recover within weeks. How is mpox spread? The mpox virus is spread through: contact with bodily fluids or skin lesions inhaling contaminated particles, such as respiratory droplets, from an infected person's mouth or throat contact with infected animals while hunting, skinning, cooking or eating contact with contaminated materials such as clothing, bedding and eating utensils Pregnant persons can pass the virus on to their unborn baby. Who is at risk of mpox? Anyone can get mpox. Children who get mpox are at higher risk of dying from the disease, especially children already weakened by malnutrition or other conditions. The DRC is the epicenter of the 2024 outbreak, with children under age 15 representing 56 percent of mpox cases reported in the country. Between January 2024 and mid-August 2024, 8,772 children were infected and 463 had died. With the DRC experiencing the largest number of suspected cases ever recorded in a single year, and with the disease spreading to several neighboring countries where it had not been found previously, the World Health Organization declared mpox a public health emergency of international concern on Aug. 14, 2024. For most people in the United States, the risk of clade 1 remains low, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How is mpox diagnosed? To test for mpox, skin or fluid samples are taken directly from the rash. According to the World Health Organization, antigen and antibody detection methods may not be useful as they do not distinguish between orthopoxviruses. What is the best way to stay protected from mpox? Avoid face-to-face, skin-to-skin, mouth-to-skin and mouth-to-mouth contact with people who have been confirmed to have the virus or who have signs and symptoms of infection. Avoid touching or sharing personal items like bedding, eating utensils, clothes, phones or other belongings of a person who has the signs and symptoms. What causes this disease, and who is at risk? The answers to these and other frequently asked questions. Updated Sept. 2, 2026 What is mpox? Mpox, also known as monkeypox, is an infectious disease caused by an orthopoxvirus. It can spread from animals to people and from person to person. Cases of mpox are most often found in areas with tropical rainforests, home to squirrels, monkeys and other small mammals that are susceptible. The virus was discovered in 1958 in Denmark in monkeys kept for research. The first reported human case of mpox was in 1970, in a 9-month-old boy in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. There are two genetic clades of the virus, clade I and clade II. Clade I mpox tends to cause a higher number of severe infections and have a higher mortality rate than clade II mpox. Most deaths occur in children. Related: Children account for half of suspected mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau How prevalent is mpox? Mpox remains a significant and ongoing global health burden. From Jan. 1, 2022 through July 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190,683 confirmed cases of mpox and 529 deaths. Roughly two-thirds of reported cases were in Africa. In 2022, there was a global outbreak of clade II mpox, which led to more than 95,000 cases across 115 non-endemic countries. The 2024 outbreak was a clade I outbreak. An upsurge of mpox cases in the DRC that year was driven by outbreaks associated with two variants of clade I, clade Ia and clade Ib. What are the symptoms of mpox? Mpox causes symptoms that are similar to smallpox, though less severe. Symptoms include skin rash, fever, sore throat, headache, body aches, back pain, low energy and swollen lymph nodes. Some people who contract mpox get very sick. Most people fully recover within weeks. How is mpox spread? The mpox virus is spread through: contact with bodily fluids or skin lesions inhaling contaminated particles, such as respiratory droplets, from an infected person's mouth or throat contact with infected animals while hunting, skinning, cooking or eating contact with contaminated materials such as clothing, bedding and eating utensils Pregnant persons can pass the virus on to their unborn baby. For most people in the United States, the risk of clade 1 remains low, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. How is mpox diagnosed? To test for mpox, skin or fluid samples are taken directly from the rash. According to the World Health Organization, antigen and antibody detection methods may not be useful as they do not distinguish between orthopoxviruses. (File photo: Department of Disease Control New cases of monkey pox (Mpox) and coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) continue to rise since June with the presence of a severer mpox strain and a low fatality rate for Covid-19, according to the Department of Disease Control. Dr Montien Kanasawat, director-general of the department, said on Wednesday that from Jan 1 to Aug 23, Thailand recorded 254 Mpox cases, including 193 cases of the Clade Ib strain and 58 cases of the Clade II strain. Patients were in Greater Bangkok, big cities and tourist provinces. Transmission resulted from sexual intercourses, which were related to visits to closed and crowded places. Dr Montien said the Mpox situation in Thailand remained controllable and the number of cases was rising for the Clade Ib strain, which caused more severe symptoms than the Clade II strain especially in patients with low immunity. Symptoms include fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes and rashes. Regarding Covid-19 infection, Dr Jurai Wongsawat, spokeswoman of the Department of Disease Control, said from Jan 1 to Aug 31 there were about 99,000 cases. Records showed that there were more cases since June due to the conditions of the wet season but total cases were lower than figures in the past three years. ADVERTISEMENT She said that the current fatality rate among Covid-19 patients was at 0.02% and most deaths were patients above the age of 60. There had not been a child fatality this year as there were enough medicine and efficient treatment systems, which limited symptoms, Dr Jurai added. Vaccination, good personal hygiene and avoiding close contact with infected people or contaminated surfaces are key to preventing both coronavirus and mpox. Covid-19 mainly spreads through respiratory droplets, whereas mpox spreads primarily through close, skin-to-skin contact. analysis.brief_en: The Bangkok Post reported on September 2, 2026, that mpox and Covid-19 cases in Thailand have continued to rise since June 2026. From January 1 to August 23, 2026, the Department of Disease Control recorded 254 mpox cases, with 193 attributed to the Clade Ib strain and 58 to the Clade II strain. The Clade Ib strain is noted for causing more severe symptoms, particularly in individuals with low immunity. Meanwhile, from January 1 to August 31, 2026, there were approximately 99,000 Covid-19 cases, with a fatality rate of 0.02%, predominantly among those over 60 years old. No child fatalities were reported for mpox this year, attributed to sufficient medical resources and effective treatment systems. The report highlights that mpox spreads primarily through close, skin-to-skin contact, while Covid-19 spreads mainly through respiratory droplets. Prevention strategies include vaccination, maintaining personal hygiene, and avoiding close contact with infected individuals or contaminated surfaces. The situation is described as controllable, with no specific mention of a fatality rate for mpox.

news.content: News Ukraine A case of monkeypox in a man has been confirmed in the Vinnytsia region UA NEWS 03 September 2026 14:27 In the Vinnytsia region, an adult man has been laboratory-confirmed to have monkeypox (mpox). The reference laboratory of the Public Health Center of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine confirmed the diagnosis. “The reference laboratory of the Public Health Center of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine has confirmed a case of monkeypox (mpox) in an adult male in the Vinnytsia region. The case is linked to a trip to European countries where this infection has been reported in recent years. There are no signs of the infection spreading in Ukraine,” the statement reads. It is noted that genetic sequencing showed that the virus belongs to clade Ib—a variant detected in EU countries. This pathogen is not new and is well known: diagnostic tests, clinical protocols, and a vaccine are available for it. The patient has a mild case of the disease, is self-isolating, and is receiving outpatient treatment. The Vinnytsia Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention conducted an epidemiological investigation and identified the circle of contacts who may have come into contact with the patient. Medical monitoring will be organized for these contacts for 21 days from the date of their last contact with the patient. The patient has received recommendations regarding self-isolation and personal hygiene. The Public Health Center, in collaboration with the Vinnytsia Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention, continues epidemiological surveillance. As previously reported, the monkeypox virus is not transmitted through the air, water, food, public transportation, or casual contact with people on the street or in a store. The virus is transmitted primarily through close, direct contact with an infected person, particularly through contact with affected skin areas, bodily fluids, and contaminated objects such as bedding, towels, clothing, etc. A significant proportion of cases are associated with close physical contact, including sexual contact. The incubation period lasts from 5 to 21 days, most commonly 6–16 days. The Public Health Center reported this on Facebook . A malaria outbreak occurred at a German airport, resulting in one death . New cases of malaria have been reported in Ukraine; here’s how to protect yourself from this dangerous disease . In Italy, the H9N2 avian flu was detected in a human for the first time in Europe . As a reminder, the new H5N1 bird flu is spreading in Germany: should we expect an epidemic? Also, Spain is imposing restrictions on poultry farms due to bird flu. A deadly strain of avian influenza has been detected for the first time in New Zealand. Read us on Telegram and Sends Download our app

analysis.brief_en: The Gay Express article titled "Mpox: A Reminder to Protect Ourselves Before the Next Outbreak" serves as a general public‐health advisory rather than a report of a specific mpox incident. It emphasizes the importance of personal protection measures and vigilance ahead of any future mpox resurgence, but it does not present any data on confirmed cases, deaths, or exposures, nor does it describe ongoing investigations, testing, or official response activities. Consequently, the article functions as guidance for the community without detailing an active outbreak or epidemiological situation.

news.source_body_en: The Gay Express article titled "Mpox: A Reminder to Protect Ourselves Before the Next Outbreak" serves as a general public‐health advisory rather than a report of a specific mpox incident. It emphasizes the importance of personal protection measures and vigilance ahead of any future mpox resurgence, but it does not present any data on confirmed cases, deaths, or exposures, nor does it describe ongoing investigations, testing, or official response activities. Consequently, the article functions as guidance for the community without detailing an active outbreak or epidemiological situation.
