news.content: About Career Advertisement Media Partnership Contact Us HOME NEWS RESEARCH LIVE DISCOURSE PERSPECTIVES AND INSIGHTS SUBMIT PRESS RELEASE NEWS DESK RESEARCH LIVE DISCOURSE PERSPECTIVES AND INSIGHTS INTERVIEW Agro-Forestry Art & Culture Technology Economy Education Energy Politics Law & Governance Health Science Social Sports Transport Urban Development WASH Home News Health Article Global Mpox Vaccine Stockpile Opens Access to Every Country Between 1 January 2022 and 31 July 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190,683 confirmed mpox cases and 529 deaths, with around two-thirds of reported infections occurring in the WHO African Region. Devdiscourse News Desk | Geneva | Updated: 03-09-2026 12:25 IST | Created: 03-09-2026 12:25 IST Representative image Image Credit: ChatGPT SHARE Key Takeaways AI Summary Analyzing article... A new global stockpile of mpox vaccines was launched on 27 August, giving every country a shared route to request doses during an outbreak, regardless of its income or purchasing power. The mechanism is expected to begin operations later this month, creating a permanent source of emergency vaccine support designed to prevent the access gaps that left many lower-income countries waiting for protection during earlier waves of the disease. A Fairer System for Emergency Vaccine Access The stockpile was approved by the Board of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, in 2025 and is being financed by Gavi, while vaccine allocation will be coordinated by the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision. The group brings together the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Médecins Sans Frontières, UNICEF and the World Health Organization, combining vaccine procurement, public health knowledge, humanitarian delivery networks and experience working directly with communities affected by disease outbreaks. The initiative grows from the Access and Allocation Mechanism created during the 2024 mpox Public Health Emergency of International Concern, when the need for faster and fairer vaccine distribution became clear. Countries facing outbreaks will now have a defined global channel through which they can seek doses based on public health need and their potential effect on controlling transmission, rather than competing in a market where wealthier buyers can secure supplies first. Mpox Remains a Threat Across the World Between 1 January 2022 and 31 July 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190,683 confirmed mpox cases and 529 deaths, with around two-thirds of reported infections occurring in the WHO African Region. The virus spreads mainly through close physical contact, while transmission from animals to people remains a concern in parts of Africa and continues to create conditions in which fresh outbreaks can emerge. Mpox can cause painful skin lesions, fever and other serious symptoms, with children and people who have weakened immune systems facing a greater risk of severe illness. Vaccination can protect people who are most exposed, reduce the chances of serious disease and help health teams bring outbreaks under control before infections spread into more communities. UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell also drew attention to the wider effect on children, including stigma, interrupted education, fear and the emotional strain caused by separation from relatives and friends. Partners Call the Stockpile a Lifesaving Step Gavi CEO Dr Sania Nishtar said the unequal vaccine access seen during the 2022 outbreak showed why a global mechanism was needed, stressing that the ability to pay should not decide which countries can use vaccines to protect lives. IFRC Secretary General and CEO Jagan Chapagain described universal access as vital, saying coordinated distribution can help doses reach communities facing the greatest danger at the time they are needed. MSF International Medical Coordinator Dr Daniela Garone said the presence of different mpox variants affecting different populations requires close cooperation among national authorities, regional bodies, disease programmes, health managers and local communities. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the stockpile an important move towards a more sustainable and equitable outbreak response, noting that quicker vaccine access can save lives and contain transmission before it expands. The initiative turns lessons from recent mpox emergencies into a standing system that countries can rely on when the next outbreak places communities at risk. Devdiscourse News Desk | Geneva | Updated: 03-09-2026 12:25 IST | Created: 03-09-2026 12:25 IST Representative image Image Credit: ChatGPT SHARE Key Takeaways AI Summary Analyzing article... A new global stockpile of mpox vaccines was launched on 27 August, giving every country a shared route to request doses during an outbreak, regardless of its income or purchasing power. The mechanism is expected to begin operations later this month, creating a permanent source of emergency vaccine support designed to prevent the access gaps that left many lower-income countries waiting for protection during earlier waves of the disease. A Fairer System for Emergency Vaccine Access The stockpile was approved by the Board of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, in 2025 and is being financed by Gavi, while vaccine allocation will be coordinated by the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision. The group brings together the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Médecins Sans Frontières, UNICEF and the World Health Organization, combining vaccine procurement, public health knowledge, humanitarian delivery networks and experience working directly with communities affected by disease outbreaks. The initiative grows from the Access and Allocation Mechanism created during the 2024 mpox Public Health Emergency of International Concern, when the need for faster and fairer vaccine distribution became clear. Countries facing outbreaks will now have a defined global channel through which they can seek doses based on public health need and their potential effect on controlling transmission, rather than competing in a market where wealthier buyers can secure supplies first. Mpox Remains a Threat Across the World Between 1 January 2022 and 31 July 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190,683 confirmed mpox cases and 529 deaths, with around two-thirds of reported infections occurring in the WHO African Region. The virus spreads mainly through close physical contact, while transmission from animals to people remains a concern in parts of Africa and continues to create conditions in which fresh outbreaks can emerge. Mpox can cause painful skin lesions, fever and other serious symptoms, with children and people who have weakened immune systems facing a greater risk of severe illness. Vaccination can protect people who are most exposed, reduce the chances of serious disease and help health teams bring outbreaks under control before infections spread into more communities. UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell also drew attention to the wider effect on children, including stigma, interrupted education, fear and the emotional strain caused by separation from relatives and friends. Partners Call the Stockpile a Lifesaving Step Gavi CEO Dr Sania Nishtar said the unequal vaccine access seen during the 2022 outbreak showed why a global mechanism was needed, stressing that the ability to pay should not decide which countries can use vaccines to protect lives. IFRC Secretary General and CEO Jagan Chapagain described universal access as vital, saying coordinated distribution can help doses reach communities facing the greatest danger at the time they are needed. MSF International Medical Coordinator Dr Daniela Garone said the presence of different mpox variants affecting different populations requires close cooperation among national authorities, regional bodies, disease programmes, health managers and local communities. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the stockpile an important move towards a more sustainable and equitable outbreak response, noting that quicker vaccine access can save lives and contain transmission before it expands. The initiative turns lessons from recent mpox emergencies into a standing system that countries can rely on when the next outbreak places communities at risk. news.content: Menu Menu Home Business Politics Nigeria International 2Open submenu Health & Wellbeing Education Life & Style Sport Editorial Backpage Close submenuInternational Africa Rest of the World Sunday, 6th September, 2026 Home Business Politics Nigeria International Africa Rest of the World Health & Wellbeing Education Life & Style Sport Editorial Backpage Search for: Breaking News Atiku, Osinbajo, Mark, Others Attend Amaechi Mother’s Burial 1 day ago Wike: I’ll Be Atiku, Obi’s Main Target If Tinubu Loses 2027 Polls 4 days ago Aliko Dangote: FG’s Reforms Driving Nigeria’s Economic Recovery, Restoring Investors’ Confidence 4 days ago Fidelity Bank Opens SME Hub, Offers Free Training to 1,000 Entrepreneurs in Kano 4 days ago Latest Headlines Sunbeth Redeems ₦25.1bn CP, Demonstrates Strong Liquidity, Investor Confidence Nigeria Escorts Koroma Home as Two-Year Political Exile Ends BNXN, Runtown, Patoranking To Storm New York For Nigeria’s 66th Independence Day Parade Adeleke’s CoS, Akinleye, Empowers Pardoned Inmates With POS Machines, Cash Global Initiative Targets Wider Access to Mpox Vaccines in Outbreak Response Nigeria | 4 days ago Shares Share Post Email Share Share Ayodeji Ake A new global initiative has been launched to improve access to mpox vaccines and ensure that countries affected by outbreaks can receive vaccines more quickly and equitably when they are needed. InfectiousDiseases The initiative builds on the work of the World Health Organisation (WHO) and its partners to strengthen international coordination of vaccine supplies and improve preparedness for mpox outbreaks, particularly in countries with limited access to vaccines. At the centre of the initiative is the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision (ICG), a mechanism established in 1997 following major meningitis outbreaks in Africa. ICG was created to coordinate emergency supplies of vaccines and antibiotics for countries facing major disease outbreaks. Its role is based on the recognition that although outbreaks are difficult to predict, timely vaccination can help prevent further transmission and reduce the impact of infectious diseases. Traditionally, ICG has been responsible for ensuring equitable access to licensed vaccines against cholera, meningitis, yellow fever, and Ebola virus disease during emergencies. Its responsibilities include managing global emergency vaccine stockpiles and working with partners, donors, and vaccine manufacturers to determine the size and composition of the stocks required for effective outbreak response. The expansion of the mechanism to include mpox is expected to provide a more structured approach to the distribution of mpox vaccines, particularly during emergencies when demand can rise rapidly. The move builds on measures introduced during the global mpox response. In 2024, WHO and its partners established an Access and Allocation Mechanism (AAM) specifically for mpox vaccines, treatments and diagnostic tests. AAM was designed to support the allocation of limited medical countermeasures to countries and communities where they were most urgently required. Under the new, longer-term arrangement, ICG will continue and strengthen the work initiated through the temporary mechanism. The development also follows a decision by the Gavi Board in 2025 to formally approve the establishment and financing of a global mpox vaccine stockpile under the long-standing ICG framework. InfectiousDiseases The stockpile is intended to ensure that vaccine supplies can be mobilised rapidly during outbreaks instead of relying solely on vaccine procurement after an emergency has already escalated. The initiative comes amid continued concern over mpox, a viral disease that can cause fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes and painful lesions. While many people recover, severe disease and death can occur, particularly among vulnerable populations. WHO has stressed the importance of vaccination as part of a broader outbreak response that also includes surveillance, testing, case management, contact tracing, infection prevention and community engagement. The global vaccine initiative is expected to complement, rather than replace, national public health measures. Health authorities and international partners will also need to address challenges around vaccine supply, financing, delivery and equitable access to ensure that the availability of a global stockpile translates into timely vaccination on the ground. The expansion of the ICG mechanism to include mpox represents a shift from short-term emergency arrangements towards a more sustainable system for vaccine preparedness. By maintaining emergency stocks and establishing clearer mechanisms for allocation, global health agencies aim to reduce delays in responding to future mpox outbreaks and ensure that countries most affected are not left behind in accessing lifesaving vaccines. news.content_zh: 一项全球性倡议已启动,以改善对猴痘 疫苗的获取,并确保在暴发期间实现公平分配。该倡议基于世界卫生组织(WHO)及其合作伙伴的工作,包括于1997年成立的国际疫苗供应协调小组(ICG),旨在协调疫苗和抗生素的紧急供应以应对疾病暴发。ICG现在将管理猴痘 疫苗的储备,建立在2024年引入的获取与分配机制(AAM)基础上。目标是减少未来猴痘 暴发响应中的延迟,并确保受影响最严重的国家不会在获取疫苗方面被落下。该倡议补充了国家公共卫生措施,并旨在解决疫苗供应、资金、配送和公平获取方面的挑战。2025年,Gavi董事会在ICG框架下批准建立了全球猴痘 疫苗储备。这一举措反映了从短期应急安排向更可持续的疫苗准备系统的转变。

September 6, 2026 Pakistan Saudi Arabia Middle East World Business Opinion Lifestyle Sport Latest News/Pakistan Pakistan says discussed advancing cooperation with Saudi Arabia, Turkiye under Makkah pact Home UK identifies 4 cases of new mpox variant, the first cluster outside Africa UK identifies 4 cases of new mpox variant, the first cluster outside Africa This colorized electron microscope image provided by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in 2024 shows Mpox virus particles, green, found within infected cultured cells, blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for differences in shape. (AP/File) Short Url https://arab.news/vsrey Scientists believe it causes milder symptoms that are harder to notice, which makes it easier to spread because people may not know they are infected Updated 7 November 2024 AP November 7, 2024 01:04 LONDON: British health officials say they have identified four cases of the new, more infectious version of mpox that first emerged in Congo, marking the first time the variant has caused a cluster of illness outside of Africa. Scientists said the risk to the public remains low. Authorities announced the first case of the new form of mpox in the UK last week, saying the case was being treated at a London hospital after recently traveling to countries in Africa with ongoing outbreaks. This week, the UK Health Security Agency said it had now identified three further cases who lived in the same household as the first patient. They too are now being treated at a hospital in London. “Mpox is very infectious in households with close contact and so it is not unexpected to see further cases within the same household,” said Susan Hopkins, chief medical adviser of the UK Health Security Agency. The new variant of mpox was first detected earlier this year in eastern Congo. Scientists believe it causes milder symptoms that are harder to notice, which makes it easier to spread because people may not know they are infected. Its spread in Congo and elsewhere in Africa prompted the World Health Organization to declare a global emergency in August. Britain recorded more than 3,000 cases of another type of mpox during a 2022 outbreak that hit more than 100 countries. The new variant of mpox has also caused outbreaks in Burundi, Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda. Single cases in travelers have also been reported in Sweden, India, Germany and Thailand. To date, there have been about 43,000 suspect cases of mpox in Africa, including more than 1,000 deaths, mostly in Congo. On Wednesday, WHO said it had allocated 899,900 vaccine doses to nine African countries struggling with mpox epidemics. news.content_zh: 英国卫生安全局已确认新猴痘变种的4例病例,标志着该变种首次在非洲以外地区出现。该变种最早于今年年初在刚果东部被发现,已在包括刚果、布隆迪、肯尼亚、卢旺达和乌干达在内的多个非洲国家引发暴发疫情,累计有超过43,000例疑似病例和超过1,000例死亡,主要集中在刚果。科学家认为该变种引起的症状较轻且不易察觉,因此更容易传播。英国的病例涉及同一家庭居住的个体,本周又发现了3例新增病例。世界卫生组织于2024年8月因该变种在非洲的传播宣布了全球紧急状态,并已向9个非洲国家分配了899,900剂疫苗疫苗。根据卫生官员的说法,公众的风险仍然较低。

Global vaccine trials to begin as Ebola and mpox spread in Africa DRC Ebola death toll reaches 3,007 as WHO chief warns of threat to wider region Nick Webster September 03, 2026 Add on Google The DR Congo Ebola outbreak has become the country's worst ever, with 3,007 deaths and 6,186 confirmed cases recorded. Global vaccine trials for Ebola's Bundibugyo strain are expected as early as next month, with the WHO coordinating efforts across affected regions. An mpox vaccine stockpile initiative, funded by Gavi, launched on August 27 to ensure lower-income countries have equitable access to shots. The UAE has restricted travel to and from African nations recording Ebola cases and previously airlifted vaccines and medical supplies to five African countries. "During the 2022 mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines," said Gavi chief executive Dr Sania Nishtar. The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the worst in the country's history, with the death toll having reached 3,007 amid an international push to develop vaccines to curb the spread of the disease. At least 6,186 cases have been confirmed in the DR Congo, with infections also spreading across its porous borders. Patients have contracted the Bundibugyo strain of the disease and the World Health Organisation said potential vaccines were to be tested to help tackle the outbreak. Trials could take place next month or in November, with other treatments also to be considered, it added. "Until every chain is found and broken, the epidemic will continue and will continue to pose a threat to DRC, its neighbours and the region as a whole," said WHO director general Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. DRC Ebola cases surpass 4,000 as officials warn of fastest spreading outbreak on record Read More The WHO formally declared the outbreak in the DRC's Ituri province on May 15. Cases have since been reported in six nearby areas. It is the worst Ebola crisis since the West African outbreak between 2014 and 2016, in which at least 28,600 people were infected and more than 11,000 died in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Travel restrictions The scale of the crisis was underlined this summer when travellers showing symptoms of Ebola were admitted to hospital in Israel after arriving from the DRC. Test results came back negative, but the incident highlighted the risks posed by international travel from areas where infections are spreading. The UAE imposed the precautionary measure of restricting travel to and from African countries that have recorded Ebola cases. Health workers bury a patient who died from Ebola in Ituri province, in the DRC. EPA Show caption: Health workers bury a patient who died from Ebola in Ituri p... Mpox outbreak Alongside the Ebola crisis, health authorities have also taken steps to improve access to mpox vaccines. An outbreak of the disease, which began in 2022, has spread to about 145 countries, with 190,683 cases and 529 deaths recorded worldwide. The Clade Ib strain has led to an increase in cases across the DRC, as well as some European countries. Mpox is much less dangerous than Ebola. About 10 per cent of cases proves deadly, compared with a fatality rate of 25 to 90 per cent for Ebola, depending on access to treatment. Both Ebola and mpox are spread differently. Mpox in transferred through close skin-to-skin contact, while Ebola is spread through contact with blood, bodily fluids or contaminated surfaces. Global vaccine stockpile A global initiative to increase a stockpile of mpox vaccines was launched on August 27, aiming to develop a long-term system to ensure countries have access to shots. It has been funded by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance in co-ordination with the International Co-ordinating Group on Vaccine Provision. “During the 2022 mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines,” said Dr Sania Nishtar, chief executive of Gavi. “It was clear that a mechanism was needed to ensure this global public good could be accessed by those who need it most. Our hope is that this stockpile will keep the world safer from the threat of this deadly disease.” In 2024, the UAE played a vital role in funding and distributing vaccines to African nations tackling mpox and Ebola cases. Shots and other medical support were flown to the DRC, Nigeria, South Africa, Ivory Coast and Cameroon. "Support is particularly important for childhood vaccination programmes," said Unicef executive director Catherine Russell. “Mpox can be devastating for children, not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends." Global vaccine trials to begin as Ebola and mpox spread in Africa DRC Ebola death toll reaches 3,007 as WHO chief warns of threat to wider region Nick Webster September 03, 2026 Add on Google The DR Congo Ebola outbreak has become the country's worst ever, with 3,007 deaths and 6,186 confirmed cases recorded. Global vaccine trials for Ebola's Bundibugyo strain are expected as early as next month, with the WHO coordinating efforts across affected regions. An mpox vaccine stockpile initiative, funded by Gavi, launched on August 27 to ensure lower-income countries have equitable access to shots. The UAE has restricted travel to and from African nations recording Ebola cases and previously airlifted vaccines and medical supplies to five African countries. "During the 2022 mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines," said Gavi chief executive Dr Sania Nishtar. The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the worst in the country's history, with the death toll having reached 3,007 amid an international push to develop vaccines to curb the spread of the disease. At least 6,186 cases have been confirmed in the DR Congo, with infections also spreading across its porous borders. Patients have contracted the Bundibugyo strain of the disease and the World Health Organisation said potential vaccines were to be tested to help tackle the outbreak. Trials could take place next month or in November, with other treatments also to be considered, it added. "Until every chain is found and broken, the epidemic will continue and will continue to pose a threat to DRC, its neighbours and the region as a whole," said WHO director general Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. DRC Ebola cases surpass 4,000 as officials warn of fastest spreading outbreak on record Read More The WHO formally declared the outbreak in the DRC's Ituri province on May 15. Cases have since been reported in six nearby areas. It is the worst Ebola crisis since the West African outbreak between 2014 and 2016, in which at least 28,600 people were infected and more than 11,000 died in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Travel restrictions The scale of the crisis was underlined this summer when travellers showing symptoms of Ebola were admitted to hospital in Israel after arriving from the DRC. Test results came back negative, but the incident highlighted the risks posed by international travel from areas where infections are spreading. The UAE imposed the precautionary measure of restricting travel to and from African countries that have recorded Ebola cases. Health workers bury a patient who died from Ebola in Ituri province, in the DRC. EPA Show caption: Health workers bury a patient who died from Ebola in Ituri p... Mpox outbreak Alongside the Ebola crisis, health authorities have also taken steps to improve access to mpox vaccines. An outbreak of the disease, which began in 2022, has spread to about 145 countries, with 190,683 cases and 529 deaths recorded worldwide. The Clade Ib strain has led to an increase in cases across the DRC, as well as some European countries. Mpox is much less dangerous than Ebola. About 10 per cent of cases proves deadly, compared with a fatality rate of 25 to 90 per cent for Ebola, depending on access to treatment. Both Ebola and mpox are spread differently. Mpox in transferred through close skin-to-skin contact, while Ebola is spread through contact with blood, bodily fluids or contaminated surfaces. Global vaccine stockpile A global initiative to increase a stockpile of mpox vaccines was launched on August 27, aiming to develop a long-term system to ensure countries have access to shots. It has been funded by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance in co-ordination with the International Co-ordinating Group on Vaccine Provision. “During the 2022 mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines,” said Dr Sania Nishtar, chief executive of Gavi. “It was clear that a mechanism was needed to ensure this global public good could be accessed by those who need it most. Our hope is that this stockpile will keep the world safer from the threat of this deadly disease.” In 2024, the UAE played a vital role in funding and distributing vaccines to African nations tackling mpox and Ebola cases. Shots and other medical support were flown to the DRC, Nigeria, South Africa, Ivory Coast and Cameroon. "Support is particularly important for childhood vaccination programmes," said Unicef executive director Catherine Russell. “Mpox can be devastating for children, not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends." supplementary_news.content_title: Targeting MPXV I7L Protease: Promising New Antiviral Strategy for, Suggests Review
supplementary_news.content: Targeting MPXV I7L Protease: Promising New Antiviral Strategy for, Suggests Review A recent clinical review published in the Indian Journal of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology in July 2026 reveals that targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease with inhibitors like A68, shikonin, and myricetin could revolutionize how clinicians combat this global health threat. Although targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease is a promising antiviral strategy, its clinical translation is hindered by poorly understood safety and selectivity profiles. To bridge this gap, Hinpetch Daungsupawong of Laos and Viroj Wiwanitkit of Saveetha University in India reviewed these key challenges to outline a clear path toward effective treatments. Therefore, the clinical review was designed as a scientific perspective and qualitative literature analysis, rather than an empirical trial, meaning it utilized no clinical population, sample size, trial duration, or clinical exclusion criteria. Instead, the authors evaluated published molecular data on I7L core protease inhibitors, focusing on translating in vitro potency to in vivo efficacy as the primary analytical endpoint. Key Clinical Findings of the Study Includes: • Inhibitor Profiles Compared: Investigators reviewed how the synthetic covalent inhibitor A68 demonstrates high in vitro potency, whereas natural compounds like shikonin and myricetin show only moderate enzymatic inhibition. • Structural Binding Gaps: Researchers highlighted that shikonin suffers from unconfirmed structural binding and poor bioavailability, while myricetin lacks specificity data against the viral protease. • Repurposing Toxicity Risks: Reviewers cautioned that repurposed compounds originally designed for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) require extensive off-target toxicity screening to prevent unintended interactions with human proteins. • In Vivo Pharmacokinetic Obstacles: Analysts emphasized that preclinical animal testing is critical to evaluate whether these promising molecules can reach therapeutic concentrations in serum and target tissues. • Synergistic Combination Therapies: Authors proposed that combining protease inhibitors with immunomodulators or vaccines can optimize treatment outcomes by simultaneously boosting immune responses and blocking replication. The results suggest that targeting the I7L core protease represents a highly viable antiviral strategy, but translating this to a clinical reality requires addressing key research gaps in structure-function relationships, in vivo pharmacokinetics, and off-target safety profiles. Expanding compound databases and implementing synergistic combination regimens will be essential steps to accelerate the delivery of safe, optimized therapies for future outbreak control. Thus, the review concludes clinicians should consider that managing monkeypox infections effectively may ultimately depend on a multi-pronged therapeutic approach that combines protease inhibitors with other antiviral strategies, such as vaccines and immunomodulatory agents, rather than relying on monotherapy. Although the review is currently limited by the lack of living-organism data for these protease inhibitors, it highlights an urgent clinical opportunity to transition these compounds into animal model testing to resolve their precise in vivo safety, bioavailability, and therapeutic dosing schedules. Reference Daungsupawong H, Wiwanitkit V. Targeting the monkeypox virus: Protease inhibitors, selectivity, and in vivo efficacy. Indian J Allergy Asthma Immunol 2026;40:9-11

Home Pakistan International Business Sports Lifestyle Sci & Tech Blogs Health Off Beat Health Karachi reports new monkeypox case By Anwar Khan - Sep 04, 2026 Add ARY News on Google Image Credit: Health News Hub AA Resize KARACHI: Another case of monkeypox has been diagnosed in Karachi, bringing the city’s total number of confirmed cases to 41, ARY News reported. A 19-year-old youth from interior Sindh was diagnosed with the disease and admitted to NIPA Hospital yesterday. A PCR test subsequently confirmed the presence of monkeypox in the young patient. The patient is currently receiving treatment in the isolation ward at NIPA Hospital. Earlier, a case of Monkeypox (mpox) had been reported in Gulistan-e-Johar, Karachi, Pakistan, according to hospital authorities. A 40-year-old man, a resident of Gulistan-e-Johar, has tested positive for the mpox virus and is currently undergoing treatment in the isolation ward (ICU) of NIPA Hospital. Hospital officials said the patient had no recent travel history. The infection was confirmed through a PCR test. With the latest case, the number of mpox patients treated at NIPA Hospital has risen to seven, while the total number of reported cases of mpox in Karachi has reached 10. Monkeypox is an illness caused by the monkeypox virus. It is a viral zoonotic infection, meaning that it can spread from animals to humans. It can also spread from humans to other humans and from the environment to humans. The monkeypox virus was discovered in Denmark (1958) in monkeys kept for research and the first reported human case of mpox was a nine-month-old boy in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC, 1970). Mpox can spread from person to person or occasionally from animals to people. Following eradication of smallpox in 1980 and the end of smallpox vaccination worldwide, mpox steadily emerged in central, east and west Africa. A global outbreak occurred in 2022–2023. The natural reservoir of the virus is unknown – various small mammals such as squirrels and monkeys are susceptible. supplementary_news.content: Sunday, September 6, 2026 Menu #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Search #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Menu Global mpox vaccine stockpile begins operations in September According to the statement, two-thirds of reported cases occurred in Africa. Olumayowa Samuel • September 2, 2026 Monkeypox used to illustrate the story [Credit: The Health Site] A global mpox vaccine stockpile will begin operations in September in a bid to ensure that all countries have access to vaccines when responding to mpox outbreaks. In a statement on Wednesday, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi), said the commencement of operations follows the launch of a global initiative to establish the stockpile on August 27, 2026. The statement read, “Set to begin operations later this month, this new global mpox vaccine stockpile that all countries can access is a resource that was approved by the Board of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi) in 2025, and is funded by Gavi and coordinated by the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. The ICG partners are the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the World Health Organization (WHO). “The initiative builds on the Access and Allocation Mechanism established in 2024 during the last mpox Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), and will ensure that countries have timely and equitable access to vaccines for outbreak response.” According to the statement, two-thirds of reported cases occurred in Africa, while from January 1, 2022, to July 31, 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190,683 confirmed cases and 529 deaths. Speaking on the development, the CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, Sania Nishtar, stated that the 2022 mpox outbreak witnessed low-income countries being left behind in terms of access to vaccines, prompting the need for a mechanism to ensure they can be accessed by those who need them most. Mr Nishtar further stated that, “Core to the Gavi Leap approach is increasing our responsiveness to country needs, and the bottom line is that any country in the world – not just those with the ability to pay the most – should be able to use this tool to save lives. “That is why Gavi supported the international response to the 2024 global mpox emergency by securing rapid access to doses through our First Response Fund, and why our Board agreed to establish and finance a global stockpile managed by our ICG partners. Our hope is that this stockpile will keep the world safer from the threat of this deadly disease.” Secretary-General and CEO of the IFRC, Jagan Chapagain, stated that, “Mpox is a horrible illness so I’m pleased that we’ve got to this important step in the battle to control it. Access to vaccines – for all who need them – is absolutely vital. That’s why this global coordination mechanism and vaccine stockpile matters. Both will help ensure vaccines reach the people and communities at greatest risk – when and where they are needed most. This is rare good news.” On her part, the International Medical Coordinator at MSF, Daniela Garone, welcomed the establishment of the vaccine stockpile under the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision, which allows for the equitable allocation of vaccines based on demand and impact in controlling disease outbreaks. Mrs Garone added, “The distinctive nature of mpox, with the coexistence of different variants that affect different populations, now demands a close collaboration between country, regional and global mechanisms as well as between disease programmes, health managers, communities and public health partners to reach more people with mpox vaccines.” UNICEF executive director Catherine Russell noted that, “Mpox can be devastating for children – not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning, and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends. This vital initiative will help us quickly get vaccines to the children, families, and communities most at risk of the disease.” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus described the launch as “an important step towards a more sustainable and equitable approach to mpox outbreak response,” adding that, “by establishing a dedicated global stockpile, using an approach that has proven successful for managing other emergency vaccines, we are ensuring that countries can access them more quickly when they need them, saving lives and containing outbreaks before they spread further.” The statement said mpox is a viral disease that spreads primarily through close physical contact between people, while animal-to-human transmission continues to occur in parts of Africa, contributing to the ongoing risk of new outbreaks. The statement explained that mpox can cause severe disease, especially in children and people with suppressed immune systems, adding that by protecting people at risk of infection and severe disease, vaccines help contain mpox outbreaks more quickly, prevent severe illness, and save lives. (File photo: Department of Disease Control New cases of monkey pox (Mpox) and coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) continue to rise since June with the presence of a severer mpox strain and a low fatality rate for Covid-19, according to the Department of Disease Control. Dr Montien Kanasawat, director-general of the department, said on Wednesday that from Jan 1 to Aug 23, Thailand recorded 254 Mpox cases, including 193 cases of the Clade Ib strain and 58 cases of the Clade II strain. Patients were in Greater Bangkok, big cities and tourist provinces. Transmission resulted from sexual intercourses, which were related to visits to closed and crowded places. Dr Montien said the Mpox situation in Thailand remained controllable and the number of cases was rising for the Clade Ib strain, which caused more severe symptoms than the Clade II strain especially in patients with low immunity. Symptoms include fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes and rashes. Regarding Covid-19 infection, Dr Jurai Wongsawat, spokeswoman of the Department of Disease Control, said from Jan 1 to Aug 31 there were about 99,000 cases. Records showed that there were more cases since June due to the conditions of the wet season but total cases were lower than figures in the past three years. She said that the current fatality rate among Covid-19 patients was at 0.02% and most deaths were patients above the age of 60. There had not been a child fatality this year as there were enough medicine and efficient treatment systems, which limited symptoms, Dr Jurai added. Vaccination, good personal hygiene and avoiding close contact with infected people or contaminated surfaces are key to preventing both coronavirus and mpox. Covid-19 mainly spreads through respiratory droplets, whereas mpox spreads primarily through close, skin-to-skin contact. Health Karachi reports new monkeypox case By Anwar Khan - Sep 04, 2026 Add ARY News on Google Image Credit: Health News Hub AA Resize KARACHI: Another case of monkeypox has been diagnosed in Karachi, bringing the city’s total number of confirmed cases to 41, ARY News reported. A 19-year-old youth from interior Sindh was diagnosed with the disease and admitted to NIPA Hospital yesterday. A PCR test subsequently confirmed the presence of monkeypox in the young patient. The patient is currently receiving treatment in the isolation ward at NIPA Hospital. Earlier, a case of Monkeypox (mpox) had been reported in Gulistan-e-Johar, Karachi, Pakistan, according to hospital authorities. A 40-year-old man, a resident of Gulistan-e-Johar, has tested positive for the mpox virus and is currently undergoing treatment in the isolation ward (ICU) of NIPA Hospital. Hospital officials said the patient had no recent travel history. The infection was confirmed through a PCR test. With the latest case, the number of mpox patients treated at NIPA Hospital has risen to seven, while the total number of reported cases of mpox in Karachi has reached 10. Monkeypox is an illness caused by the monkeypox virus. It is a viral zoonotic infection, meaning that it can spread from animals to humans. It can also spread from humans to other humans and from the environment to humans. The monkeypox virus was discovered in Denmark (1958) in monkeys kept for research and the first reported human case of mpox was a nine-month-old boy in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC, 1970). Mpox can spread from person to person or occasionally from animals to people. Following eradication of smallpox in 1980 and the end of smallpox vaccination worldwide, mpox steadily emerged in central, east and west Africa. A global outbreak occurred in 2022–2023. The natural reservoir of the virus is unknown – various small mammals such as squirrels and monkeys are susceptible. supplementary_news.content_title: Kenya to receive mpox vaccines from stockpile
supplementary_news.content: A person suffering from Mpox/FILE Kenya will benefit from a new global stockpile of Mpox vaccines that will help countries get the jabs faster when outbreaks occur. The stockpile was launched on August 27 and is expected to begin operations later this month. It has been created to make sure that countries can get Mpox vaccines quickly and fairly, especially when infections start rising. The initiative is funded by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and will be coordinated by the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. The ICG brings together the World Health Organisation, Unicef, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and Médecins Sans Frontières. “During the 2022 Mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines," Gavi CEO Dr Sania Nishtar said. "It was clear that a mechanism was needed to ensure this global public good could be accessed by those who need it most.” WHO director general Dr Tedros Ghebreyesus called the launch an important step towards a more sustainable and equitable approach to fighting Mpox outbreaks. “By establishing a dedicated global stockpile, using an approach that has proven successful for managing other emergency vaccines, we are ensuring that countries can access them more quickly when they need them, saving lives and containing outbreaks before they spread further,” he said. Kenya's own experience with Mpox shows why this matters. Earlier this year, WHO data showed Kenya recording the highest number of Mpox deaths in Africa over a six-week stretch between February and March 2026, even though the country did not have the most cases. Four people died out of 78 confirmed cases in that period alone. However, the most recent WHO report, published on July 31, paints a somewhat different picture. Over the six weeks leading up to July 19, Kenya recorded 48 confirmed Mpox cases and no deaths, placing it third among African countries after Madagascar and Angola. This suggests Kenya's outbreak has eased compared to earlier in the year, even though it remains among the countries WHO is watching closely. Madagascar remains by far the worst-hit country on the continent. It has reported nearly 3,000 confirmed cases and 18 deaths since December 2025, the largest Mpox outbreak anywhere in Africa or the world right now. The island nation has vaccinated close to 90,000 people, including health workers, sex workers and people living with HIV, though the outbreak is not yet under control. Across Africa as a whole, 32 countries reported more than 51,000 confirmed Mpox cases and 235 deaths between January 2025 and mid-July 2026. Globally, Mpox has affected 105 countries, with more than 63,000 confirmed cases and 256 deaths recorded since the start of 2025. Mpox spreads mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including through sex, and sometimes through contact with infected animals. It can cause fever, painful skin rashes and swollen lymph nodes. The illness can be especially dangerous for young children and people with weak immune systems, such as those living with untreated HIV. Health officials say vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to protect people at high risk and stop outbreaks from spreading further. With the new global stockpile now in place, Kenya and other African countries facing Mpox outbreaks should find it easier and faster to get vaccine doses when they are needed, rather than competing with wealthier nations for limited supplies. WHO urged countries, including Kenya, to strengthen surveillance, expand testing and keep the public informed, as the disease continues to circulate in communities across the continent. Health experts note that Mpox spreads more easily where surveillance is weak and testing is limited, meaning true case numbers in some counties could be higher than what is officially reported. “Mpox can be devastating for children, not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends," Unicef executive director Catherine Russell said. "This vital initiative will help us quickly get vaccines to the children, families and communities most at risk of the disease."

Malawi Formally Ends Cholera and Mpox Outbreaks The formal end to these health crises was determined by specific epidemiological benchmarks. Malawi's health authorities have officially announced the cessation of both the cholera and mpox outbreaks that had affected the nation. This significant declaration follows a period of rigorous public health interventions and successful containment strategies across the country. The formal end to these health crises was determined by specific epidemiological benchmarks. For cholera, the declaration came after more than 28 consecutive days passed without any new laboratory-confirmed cases being recorded. Similarly, the mpox outbreak was declared over after a sustained period of over 90 days with no new cases identified. These critical milestones underscore the effectiveness of the national response in managing and ultimately bringing these widespread diseases under control. The announcement brings a collective sense of relief to the Malawian populace, signaling a return to normalcy after a challenging period of public health concern. Regulatory Landscape Shifts Following Health Emergency Declarations The official declaration by the Malawi Ministry of Health regarding the end of the cholera and mpox outbreaks carries significant implications for the country's regulatory environment. Historically, such public health emergencies often necessitate the implementation of various emergency health regulations, restrictions, or specific compliance measures to curb disease transmission and protect public welfare. With the current Malawi public health outbreak status now cleared, a review of these mandates is anticipated. Legal and compliance professionals should now actively monitor for official directives concerning the repeal or modification of any previously enacted public health orders. Businesses and organizations that adapted their operations or implemented specific protocols in response to the outbreaks may find these requirements are no longer in effect. Advising clients on the cessation of these specific compliance obligations will be crucial as the Malawi health emergency is effectively lifted. This transition period requires careful attention to ensure that all parties are aware of the evolving legal landscape and can adjust their practices accordingly. The formal declaration provides a clear signal for stakeholders to assess their current operational frameworks against the updated regulatory environment, ensuring continued adherence to national health guidelines while shedding any no-longer-necessary restrictions. A Significant Public Health Achievement for Malawi The successful containment and subsequent declaration of the end of both cholera and mpox outbreaks represent a substantial public health achievement for Malawi. This dual victory highlights the resilience of the nation's health systems and the dedication of its health workers in confronting and overcoming significant epidemiological challenges. The rigorous monitoring and intervention efforts that led to the absence of new cases for extended periods demonstrate a robust and effective response. Beyond the immediate health benefits, the cessation of these outbreaks paves the way for broader societal and economic recovery. Communities can now fully focus on rebuilding and resuming normal activities without the pervasive threat of these diseases. This milestone reinforces the importance of sustained investment in public health infrastructure and preparedness to safeguard against future health crises, ensuring the continued well-being and prosperity of the Malawian people. Practical Implications The declaration of the end of these outbreaks signals the potential lifting of emergency health regulations or restrictions. Lawyers and compliance officers should advise clients on the cessation of any specific compliance measures or operational adjustments previously mandated due to these outbreaks, and monitor for official repeal of related public health directives. supplementary_news.content: Three new monkeypox cases reported from Karachi Monkeypox has resurfaced in Sindh province with three new confirmed cases, including a man and his daughter, pushing the provincial tally to 40, according to 24NewsHD TV channel on Friday. According to hospital sources at Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital in NIPA, PCR tests confirmed Mpox in three patients currently under treatment. One additional suspected case has been reported and test results are awaited. Of the three newly confirmed cases, two patients belong to interior Sindh and are a father and daughter. The third confirmed patient is a 46-year-old man from Karachi's Federal B Area. Officials said the final situation will be clear once the report of the suspected patient is received. With the latest cases, the total number of confirmed Mpox cases in the province has reached 40, including 13 from Karachi. Health experts said Mpox is a viral disease caused by a virus from the same family as the smallpox virus. The prominent symptoms include rash, painful or itchy lesions, fever, headache, body aches and fatigue. In some patients, lymph nodes in the neck, armpits or groin may also swell. The Mpox rash can appear on different parts of the body, including the face, hands, feet, mouth and throat. Some patients may not show any clear symptoms before the lesions appear. It can take up to 21 days for symptoms to appear after exposure to the virus. Reporter: Ibrahim Rind

According to a joint statement released by the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organisation (WHO), Malawi has recorded zero laboratory-confirmed cholera cases for over 28 consecutive days, alongside zero mpox cases for more than 90 consecutive days. The achievement marks the end of a rigorous outbreak control effort that saw health officials manage 3 200 cholera cases across 18 affected districts and isolate 162 confirmed mpox cases nationwide. Despite reaching the official containment thresholds, the Ministry of Health has urged local communities to maintain strict standards of hygiene and remain vigilant to prevent any resurgence of either disease. –ChannelAfrica– Search Search Home NEWS FINANCE SPORT SHOWS PRESENTER PROFILE PROGRAMME SCHEDULE Languages CHINYANJA FRENCH PORTUGUESE KISWAHILI LIFESTYLE & ENTERTAINMENT Lifestyle & Entertainment Events MUSIC PODCAST & CATCH-UP PODCAST CATCH-UP COMPETITIONS AND POLLS COMPETITIONS POLLS SPECIAL PROJECTS ADVERTISE ABOUT US CONTACT US

Targeting MPXV I7L Protease: Promising New Antiviral Strategy for, Suggests Review Written By : Aashi verma Published On 2026-09-02T21:00:02+05:30 | Updated On 3 Sept 2026 2:59 PM IST A recent clinical review published in the Indian Journal of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology in July 2026 reveals that targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease with inhibitors like A68, shikonin, and myricetin could revolutionize how clinicians combat this global health threat. Although targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease is a promising antiviral strategy, its clinical translation is hindered by poorly understood safety and selectivity profiles. To bridge this gap, Hinpetch Daungsupawong of Laos and Viroj Wiwanitkit of Saveetha University in India reviewed these key challenges to outline a clear path toward effective treatments. Therefore, the clinical review was designed as a scientific perspective and qualitative literature analysis, rather than an empirical trial, meaning it utilized no clinical population, sample size, trial duration, or clinical exclusion criteria. Instead, the authors evaluated published molecular data on I7L core protease inhibitors, focusing on translating in vitro potency to in vivo efficacy as the primary analytical endpoint. Key Clinical Findings of the Study Includes: • Inhibitor Profiles Compared: Investigators reviewed how the synthetic covalent inhibitor A68 demonstrates high in vitro potency, whereas natural compounds like shikonin and myricetin show only moderate enzymatic inhibition. • Structural Binding Gaps: Researchers highlighted that shikonin suffers from unconfirmed structural binding and poor bioavailability, while myricetin lacks specificity data against the viral protease. • Repurposing Toxicity Risks: Reviewers cautioned that repurposed compounds originally designed for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) require extensive off-target toxicity screening to prevent unintended interactions with human proteins. • In Vivo Pharmacokinetic Obstacles: Analysts emphasized that preclinical animal testing is critical to evaluate whether these promising molecules can reach therapeutic concentrations in serum and target tissues. • Synergistic Combination Therapies: Authors proposed that combining protease inhibitors with immunomodulators or vaccines can optimize treatment outcomes by simultaneously boosting immune responses and blocking replication. The results suggest that targeting the I7L core protease represents a highly viable antiviral strategy, but translating this to a clinical reality requires addressing key research gaps in structure-function relationships, in vivo pharmacokinetics, and off-target safety profiles. Expanding compound databases and implementing synergistic combination regimens will be essential steps to accelerate the delivery of safe, optimized therapies for future outbreak control. Thus, the review concludes clinicians should consider that managing monkeypox infections effectively may ultimately depend on a multi-pronged therapeutic approach that combines protease inhibitors with other antiviral strategies, such as vaccines and immunomodulatory agents, rather than relying on monotherapy. Although the review is currently limited by the lack of living-organism data for these protease inhibitors, it highlights an urgent clinical opportunity to transition these compounds into animal model testing to resolve their precise in vivo safety, bioavailability, and therapeutic dosing schedules. Reference Daungsupawong H, Wiwanitkit V. Targeting the monkeypox virus: Protease inhibitors, selectivity, and in vivo efficacy. Indian J Allergy Asthma Immunol 2026;40:9-11.
